subset.criteria: Within each effective category, prioritize foundational problems, breadth of consequences, historical standing, and distinct directions. The existing editorial importance scores and focus notes informed the ordering. Solution status, solver identity, forecast dates, and hypothetical solves were excluded as criteria.

shared_definitions.scope: Shared terminology for the green selection reviewed on 20 November 2026. Each card specifies its input representation, parameters and cost model.

entries.title: How to read the shared definitions
entries.text:
Write \(N=|\langle X\rangle|\) for the length in bits of an encoded instance \(X\). On a SAT card, \(n\) usually counts variables. On a graph card, \(n\) usually counts vertices. Read the local definition before substituting either quantity into a bound. A truth table on \(n\) variables, for example, occupies \(2^n\) bits before a threshold or header is added.

For a Boolean function \(f\), \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathcal B}(f)\) denotes its minimum circuit size under the named basis and cost convention. A given circuit \(C\) has size \(s=|C|\). For a language \(L\), \(L_n\) is its characteristic function on \(n\)-bit strings. De Morgan formula leaf size is \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\).

A card's local definitions specify its model, promises and exceptions. The linked entries supply shared terminology, also available in the JSON exports.

entries.title: Input encodings and size parameters
entries.text:
For a finitely encoded object \(X\), write \(\langle X\rangle\) for its binary description and \(N=|\langle X\rangle|\) for its complete bit length. Count signs, indices, delimiters, coefficients and all explicitly supplied lists. An explicit table or syntax tree is supplied in full; a circuit or oracle generating it is a different representation. The card specifies the representation and the treatment of malformed inputs or inputs outside a promise.

Unless a card states otherwise, integer data in a bit model are binary, and rational data are signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Unary input is an explicit exception, as for some security parameters. The magnitude of an integer is not its bit length. An algorithm polynomial in numerical magnitude may take exponential time in a binary description.

Polynomial-time decidability is invariant under encodings interconvertible in polynomial time with polynomial output length. This does not preserve a precise exponent, a linear or quasilinear bound, or a circuit-size threshold. For those targets, retain the specific encoding and account for conversion costs. Bounds in a structural parameter must also account for the full supplied input; they are not promises of that running time for arbitrarily padded descriptions. An oracle, streaming, query or exact-real model has its own explicitly stated input-access costs.

entries.title: Asymptotic bounds and quantifiers
entries.text:
All unspecified logarithms have base two. \(f(n)=O(g(n))\) means that some constant \(C>0\) bounds \(f(n)\le Cg(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\); \(f=o(g)\) means \(f(n)/g(n)\to0\) where the ratio is defined. A polynomial bound has a fixed exponent and coefficient. Constants may depend on parameters declared fixed by the card, but not on varying instances.

Failure of a polynomial upper bound means that every proposed polynomial is exceeded at arbitrarily large lengths. It does not automatically mean a superpolynomial lower bound at every sufficiently large length. Preserve the displayed quantifier order. Likewise, a single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time algorithm and a separate \(2^{\varepsilon n}\)-time algorithm for each \(\varepsilon>0\) are not interchangeable without further conditions.

\(\operatorname{poly}(N)\) denotes some fixed polynomial factor. In SAT bounds such as \(2^{o(n)}\operatorname{poly}(N)\), \(n\) counts variables and \(N\) counts encoding bits. The meaning of \(\widetilde O\) and the parameters inside its suppressed logarithmic factors must follow the individual card.

entries.title: Uniform computation and bit cost
entries.text:
In the bit model, a uniform deterministic algorithm is one finite Turing-machine program for all input lengths, using a fixed number of tapes and finite tape alphabets. Each transition costs one step. Input access, integer arithmetic, auxiliary computation and writing output count. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) on every input of length \(N\), for fixed \(C,k\). The program receives no length-dependent advice or oracle unless the card explicitly supplies one.

A nondeterministic machine accepts when at least one branch accepts. A nondeterministic time bound applies to every branch. A randomized time guarantee and an expected-time guarantee are distinguished in the randomization entry. Polynomial-time class comparisons are robust under the usual polynomial-overhead machine simulations; precise time bounds must retain the machine model selected by the card.

entries.title: Languages, P, NP and coNP
entries.text:
A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\). Membership is a total yes/no question, including the empty string. Its characteristic function at length \(n\) is \(L_n(x)=1\) exactly when \(x\in L\).

\(\mathrm{P}\) is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithms in the bit model. A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a polynomial \(p\) and one deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:\ V(x,y)=1.\]
The verifier halts on every pair, with time polynomial in \(|x|+|y|\); it accepts no allowed witness on a no-instance. The program and bounds are fixed independently of \(x\). This is equivalent to nondeterministic polynomial time. A language belongs to \(\mathrm{coNP}\) exactly when its complement in \(\{0,1\}^*\) belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\). These are language classes; witness-output and promise problems require their own definitions.

entries.title: Decision and search reductions
entries.text:
A polynomial-time many-one (Karp) reduction from \(A\) to \(B\) is one total uniform deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) satisfying \(x\in A\iff f(x)\in B\). It writes one entire target instance. A language is NP-hard under these reductions when every NP language reduces to it, and NP-complete when it is also in NP. Other completeness notions must name their reduction type.

For search relations \(R,Q\), a polynomial-time many-one search reduction consists of two polynomial-time maps \(F,G\). The output instance must belong to the target domain for every input in the source domain. For every such input \(x\) and every valid answer \(z\) to \(Q\) on \(F(x)\), one requires \(R(x,G(x,z))\). Time is measured in \(|x|\) for \(F\) and \(|x|+|z|\) for \(G\). Correctness must hold for every accepted target answer. Domain and malformed-input conventions remain local.

A Turing reduction may instead make adaptive oracle queries. Logarithmic-space, randomized, promise-preserving and count-preserving reductions are separate notions. Do not replace one by another when normalizing wording.

entries.title: SAT, CNF-SAT, k-SAT and Circuit-SAT
entries.text:
SAT asks whether an explicitly encoded Boolean formula has a satisfying assignment. A formula is a finite tree over variables, constants 0 and 1, binary AND and OR, and unary NOT. Repeated subexpressions are written separately. A literal is a variable or its negation. A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals. In this glossary, \(k\)-CNF means at most \(k\) literals per clause; an exactly-\(k\) convention must be stated locally. An empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false.

\(n\) counts variables, \(m\) counts clauses when applicable, and \(N\) is the full encoding length. Binary variable indices and delimiters contribute to \(N\). SAT, CNF-SAT and 3-SAT are polynomial-time interreducible, but a reduction may change the number of variables and the precise running-time bound. A card's restricted syntax, numbering and padding rules remain part of its problem.

Circuit-SAT receives a circuit DAG, which can share subcomputations. This is not a formula tree. MCSP instead receives a full truth table of length \(2^n\), together with its size threshold. A clause-incidence encoding of 3-SAT is another explicitly identified representation. Never identify these input lengths.

entries.title: Boolean circuits and minimum circuit size
entries.text:
A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input wires and one or more ordered outputs. Gate values can be reused; fan-out and depth are unrestricted unless restricted locally. Correctness is exact on the card's entire domain, or on its stated promise set. Circuits for different lengths are nonuniform unless a uniform constructor is explicitly required.

In the \(\mathrm{DM}\) convention, gates are binary AND and OR and unary NOT. All operation gates, including NOT, cost one; input wires, constant sources 0 and 1, wires and output designations are free. An output may be an input, a constant or a gate. In the \(B_2\) convention, any Boolean function of at most two input bits is a unit-cost gate, with the same free sources and wires. Write \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) or \(\operatorname{CC}_{B_2}(f)\) for the minimum gate count. Multiple outputs share one joint budget.

The subscript \(\mathcal B\) in \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathcal B}\) records the basis and cost convention. In the \(\mathrm{DM+c}\) convention, constants are gates of cost one and the other De Morgan costs are the same. For a language, apply it to \(L_n\), not to the infinite language without specifying a length. \(s=|C|\) denotes the size of a given circuit, not a minimum. Fixed complete bounded-fan-in bases preserve polynomial size and linear-size existence up to constant factors; they do not preserve exact optimum sizes or exact MCSP thresholds.

A threshold-circuit card specifies how a majority gate treats an even tie and whether size charges wires. Each occurrence of a repeated input counts separately when wires are charged. Modular gates and unbounded fan-in also require a named basis. Use the card's cost convention when comparing exact size thresholds.

entries.title: De Morgan formulas and leaf size
entries.text:
A De Morgan formula is a rooted tree with binary AND/OR and unary NOT operations, variable leaves and optional constants. Internal computations cannot be shared. The size convention \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) is the minimum number of variable-leaf occurrences in a formula computing \(f\) exactly. Positive and negative occurrences each count, including repeated occurrences of the same variable. Constant leaves are free. Constants have size zero and a literal has size one. Pushing negations to the leaves preserves this measure.

Formula leaf size, circuit gate count and circuit depth are distinct measures. A source may call formula size \(L(f)\) and circuit size \(S(f)\); revised cards use \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) and \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) while retaining original symbols in source quotations. Restricted, arithmetic or other formula models must retain their own cost conventions.

entries.title: L, NL and PSPACE
entries.text:
Space is the number of work-tape cells visited, with fixed finite alphabets; the read-only input is not charged. The classes \(\mathrm{L}\) and \(\mathrm{NL}\) use deterministic and nondeterministic machines, respectively, with \(O(\log(N+2))\) workspace. Nondeterministic acceptance is existential over branches; a polynomial clock can be imposed for NL. A halting deterministic logspace machine has only polynomially many configurations and therefore polynomial running time.

\(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) consists of languages decided by halting deterministic machines with polynomial workspace. It imposes no polynomial time bound. Read-only input, output-tape access, catalytic storage and other auxiliary memory conventions must not be changed when a card specifies a different space model.

entries.title: EXP, NEXP and their complements
entries.text:
\(\mathrm{EXP}\), also called \(\mathrm{EXPTIME}\), is deterministic time \(2^{N^{O(1)}}\), the union over fixed polynomial exponents. \(\mathrm{NEXP}\) is the corresponding nondeterministic class, with every branch time-bounded. Equivalent bounds can be written \(C2^{(N+1)^k}\) for fixed positive integers \(C,k\). \(\mathrm{coNEXP}\) consists of complements of NEXP languages. Machines are uniform and have no advice unless a suffix explicitly supplies it.

\(\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{O(N)})\) and \(\mathrm{NE}=\mathrm{NTIME}(2^{O(N)})\) have linear exponents. They are distinct definitions from EXP and NEXP; any use of padding to relate particular containment questions must be justified locally.

entries.title: BPP, RP and randomized guarantees
entries.text:
\(\mathrm{BPP}\) consists of languages decided by one uniform randomized Turing machine in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, with error at most \(1/3\) on each individual input. Random bits are independent and unbiased. \(\mathrm{RP}\) has the same worst-case time convention, never accepts a no-instance, and accepts each yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). Constant error thresholds can be amplified within polynomial time.

A Las Vegas algorithm is always correct whenever it outputs and terminates with probability one; a claimed expected-time bound averages over its internal randomness for each fixed input. This differs from a worst-case bound on every random tape. A Monte Carlo guarantee permits a stated error probability. Average-case input distributions, simultaneous correctness over a sequence of queries, and adaptive adversaries are specified locally. Do not turn any of these into a blanket BPP guarantee.

entries.title: Nonuniformity, P/poly and advice
entries.text:
\(\mathrm{P/poly}\) consists of languages whose functions \(L_n\) have Boolean circuits of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\), for constants depending on the language. One circuit is chosen for each length; no computable circuit generator is required. This is equivalent to deterministic polynomial time with a polynomial-length advice string \(a_n\) depending only on the input length.

More generally, a suffix /poly supplies polynomial-length advice that is fixed before the instance is chosen. Advice need not be computable. For NEXP/poly, the nondeterministic running time is exponential in a polynomial of the original input length. The familiar equality of some advised classes does not establish the equality of their uniform versions. Any circuit uniformity condition, oracle, shared randomness or input-dependent information is a separate model choice.

entries.title: FP, #P and total NP search
entries.text:
FP denotes total functions computed by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines, with output bits charged. A nonnegative integer output is written in binary unless stated otherwise. A #P function has the form
\[f(x)=|\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\}|,\]
where \(p\) is a polynomial and \(V\) a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Count distinct witness strings, even if several represent the same object. Padding must preserve these counts; ordinary existence-preserving NP reductions need not do so.

TFNP concerns polynomially balanced, polynomial-time decidable relations \(R(x,y)\) with at least one valid answer for every input. A polynomial-time algorithm for a search relation selects some valid answer. This relation-solving usage of FP is explicitly identified on search cards. Search, decision and exact counting are different tasks.

entries.title: Word RAM, real RAM and oracle access
entries.text:
A word RAM stores words of the bit width stated by the card, usually \(\Theta(\log(n+2))\). Each card lists its finite set of unit-cost instructions or explicitly selects the integer instructions below. The availability of multiplication, division, random words, packed input and precomputed tables is not inferred from the name alone. Multiword arithmetic is charged by its component operations. A polynomial-time equivalence with Turing machines does not justify transferring a precise exponent without overhead.

Integer instructions for cards that explicitly select them. On unsigned \(w\)-bit words, allow addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, comparison, copying, branching, and random-access reads and writes. Each costs one step. A shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Multiword operations cost their component steps. A memory instruction accesses one word. Random bits or words, and the cost of generating them, are specified by the individual card.

A real RAM or algebraic model may charge exact operations on reals at unit cost. It is not a bit-cost algorithm on arbitrary precision rational data. Query and oracle models charge the specified accesses and may deliberately leave the oracle's internal computation uncharged. Streaming passes, online deadlines and data-structure preprocessing and queries keep their local costs.

entries.title: Arithmetic circuits and field conventions
entries.text:
An arithmetic circuit is a DAG computing a polynomial through arithmetic operations over the specified field or ring. Unless a card explicitly uses a different notion, polynomial equality means equality as formal polynomials, not agreement only on selected evaluation points. The field, permitted constants, division gates, commutativity and size measure are part of the model.

Boolean \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathcal B}\) does not stand for arithmetic circuit complexity. Arithmetic cards keep a field-qualified local notation and explicitly say whether they count input gates, operation gates, wires, or some combination. Arbitrary field constants of unit cost do not have the same meaning as finitely encoded binary constants. Changing among these conventions can preserve some asymptotic questions but requires checking the target; no global change of field, constants or uniformity is made here.

entries.title: Security parameters and negligible functions
entries.text:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\) when not locally rebound, and unary \(1^\lambda\) input is used when the card specifies it. Polynomial security bounds are in \(\lambda\), not in the bit length of a binary spelling of \(\lambda\). A nonnegative function \(\nu\) is negligible if, for every constant \(c>0\), \(\nu(\lambda)<\lambda^{-c}\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\).

The adversary's uniformity, advice, auxiliary input, oracle access, interaction and probability space are specified by the security experiment. A polynomial-size circuit adversary is not the same model as a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machine. Information-theoretic, statistical and computational guarantees must retain their quantifiers and error parameters.

entries.title: Graphs and structural size
entries.text:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\) are structural counts, not automatically its bit length. The card specifies whether edges are directed, loops or parallel edges are allowed, and whether labels, weights and a distinguished vertex form part of the input.

Adjacency matrices, adjacency lists and edge lists are different encodings. Binary endpoints typically cost logarithmically many bits, and binary weights contribute their full bit lengths. Query access to adjacency is another model. Graphs used as mathematical objects in an existence question need not be algorithmic inputs at all. No global simplicity, connectivity or representation assumption is imposed by a link to this entry.

entries.title: The polynomial hierarchy and TQBF
entries.text:
Set \(\Sigma_0^{\mathrm P}=\Pi_0^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm P\). For fixed \(k\ge1\), membership in \(L\in\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\) is expressed by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(R\) and a polynomial \(p\). For each input \(x\), choose \(k\) strings of length \(p(|x|)\) under alternating quantifiers, starting with an existential quantifier. Then \(x\in L\) exactly when the resulting quantified predicate \(R(x,y_1,\ldots,y_k)\) is true. A block quantifies an entire string. \(\Pi_k^{\mathrm P}\) consists of the complements of these languages, and \(\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup_{k\ge0}\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\). The level, polynomial and predicate are fixed for the language.

TQBF is the language of true, fully quantified Boolean formulas. Every variable in the Boolean matrix is bound by the prefix, each quantifier ranges over one bit, and malformed encodings are rejected. The number of blocks in an input can grow with its length. TQBF is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions.

entries.title: Parameterized time and reductions
entries.text:
A parameterized instance has a finite description and a distinguished nonnegative integer \(k\). Let \(N\) be the complete encoded length. A fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) decision algorithm runs in \(f(k)(N+1)^c\) steps for a total computable \(f\) and one constant \(c\) independent of \(k\). The card fixes how the parameter is encoded. A polynomial exponent that may depend on \(k\) gives a different guarantee.

An FPT many-one reduction computes an equivalent target instance \((x',k')\) within such a time bound and guarantees \(k'\le g(k)\) for a total computable \(g\). Kernelization additionally uses polynomial preprocessing time and bounds the size of the resulting instance as a function of \(k\).

entries.title: Finite words and finite automata
entries.text:
An alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite set of symbols. The set \(\Sigma^*\) contains all finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Word length counts symbols. A complete one-way deterministic finite automaton has a finite state set \(Q\) and transition function \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\). Its extension to words starts at the given state and reads symbols from left to right. Acceptance uses an initial state and a set of final states when the task calls for a language.

A nondeterministic automaton can have several transitions. A word is accepted if it has an accepting run. Unambiguity permits at most one accepting run per word. Two-way heads, endmarkers, empty moves, and acceptance of infinite words use the conventions on the individual card.

entries.title: Approximation ratios and rounding
entries.text:
For a minimization problem with nonnegative costs, a factor \(\alpha\ge1\) bounds the cost of a feasible output by \(\alpha\,\operatorname{OPT}\). For a nonnegative maximization problem a card may use a fraction \(\rho\in[0,1]\) and require value at least \(\rho\,\operatorname{OPT}\). The inequality also specifies the guarantee when the optimum is zero. An additive error has the units of the objective.

For a randomized algorithm, read whether the inequality holds in expectation or with a specified probability on each instance. Expected cost and expected running time concern different random quantities. For a minimization relaxation with a positive lower bound, its integrality gap is the supremum of the integral-to-relaxed optimum ratio over the stated instances. An algorithmic target also counts the cost of finding a feasible solution.

entries.title: Total variation and mixing time
entries.text:
The total variation distance between probability laws \(\mu,
u\) on the same measurable space is \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,
u)=\sup_A|\mu(A)-
u(A)|\), where \(A\) ranges over measurable events. On a finite state space \(\Omega\) it equals \(	frac12\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\mu(x)-
u(x)|\).

For a discrete-time Markov chain with transition matrix \(P\) and stationary law \(\pi\), the worst-start mixing time at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is the least \(t\ge0\) with \(\max_x d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P^t(x,\cdot),\pi)\le\varepsilon\), or infinity if there is no such time. A transition, a whole sweep and one unit of continuous time have different costs. The card fixes the clock, starting law and tolerance.

entries.title: Online cost and competitive ratio
entries.text:
An online rule sees requests in arrival order. At time \(t\) it may use the observed prefix and its allowed internal state. The offline optimum knows the full sequence and obeys the resource and feasibility constraints specified for it. For a minimization problem, a typical competitive bound is \(\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+b\). The card says whether an additive constant is allowed and what it may depend on.

For a randomized rule and an oblivious adversary, the request sequence is fixed independently of the random bits. Expected cost is then taken for each such sequence. Random-order input, adaptive adversaries and regret against a fixed comparator define different guarantees.

entries.title: Streaming passes and memory
entries.text:
A stream supplies a sequence of records. A pass is one traversal in the stated order. In a one-pass algorithm, later computation can use an earlier record only through information saved when it was available. Space counts bits or words according to the card, including any retained seeds or buffers that its model charges.

An insertion-only stream, a stream with deletions and a uniformly random permutation of a fixed multiset give different inputs. Read the local convention for order, precision, success probability, permitted preprocessing and the size of the output.

entries.title: The cell-probe model
entries.text:
A data structure stores information in cells of \(w\) bits. A query may choose its next address using the query and values returned by earlier probes. Reading or writing a cell counts as a probe under the local rules. Computation between probes is free. Space counts available cells, or their bits if specified.

The card sets \(w\), the allowed preprocessing, private state, and any randomness. In a static problem the stored data do not change between queries. A dynamic problem specifies updates and whether the bound applies to each operation or is amortized over a sequence.

entries.title: Learning error, examples and confidence
entries.text:
For a classifier \(h\) and a joint law \(D\) of labeled examples, its zero-one error is \(\Pr_{(X,Y)\sim D}[h(X)\ne Y]\). In a realizable problem, the target class contains a hypothesis with zero error. An agnostic excess-error guarantee compares the output with the infimum of the error over the reference class. A proper learner must return a member of that class.

The confidence statement concerns the training sample and the learner's own randomness. The output's prediction error concerns a fresh draw from the specified distribution. The card fixes the sampling or query access, distribution family, loss, and whether time includes evaluating the returned hypothesis.

entries.title: Uniform quantum computation and BQP
entries.text:
A BQP computation decides a language using a uniform polynomial-size family of quantum circuits over a fixed efficiently specified universal gate set, with acceptance probability at least \(2/3\) on yes-inputs and at most \(1/3\) on no-inputs. Repetition with fresh work registers can reduce the error. The uniform constructor and input encoding are part of the model.

A quantum query counts an invocation of the specified oracle. A channel capacity, a quantum proof system and the distinguishing power of a restricted gate set each require their own resource and success definitions.

entries.title: Unit-cost string edit distance
entries.text:
For finite strings \(x,y\), their unit-cost edit distance is the smallest number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform \(x\) into \(y\). Identical symbols may be matched at zero cost. Length counts symbols. The alphabet, representation, and the resource used to read each symbol are given locally.

An approximation to this distance, an edit script, and aligning more than two strings are different outputs. Tree edits and insertion/deletion-only metrics have their own local operations.

entries.title: Finite relational structures and conjunctive queries
entries.text:
A finite relational signature lists relation symbols and their arities. A structure interprets an \(r\)-ary symbol as a set of ordered \(r\)-tuples on its domain. A homomorphism maps elements of one structure into the other so that every tuple present in a relation maps to a tuple in the same relation. A conjunctive query existentially quantifies a conjunction of relational atoms, leaving any answer variables free.

Under set semantics a tuple is either present or absent. Under bag semantics occurrences carry multiplicity. Data complexity fixes the schema and query and varies the database. Combined complexity can include the query as input. The card specifies which objects vary, its access model and the semantics of constraints, answers or repairs.

entries.title: The SAT encoding for ETH and SETH
entries.text:
For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(b\) be the length of the binary expansion of \(a+1\). Define \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\,\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\). Codes are self-delimiting. With a fixed width bound \(q\ge3\), encode a CNF by \(\operatorname{code}(n)\), \(\operatorname{code}(m)\), then the \(m\) clauses in list order. A clause begins with its coded literal count. Each literal has a sign bit (zero for positive) and a coded index from \(1\) through \(n\). Every declared variable must occur. A clause may contain up to \(q\) literals, including zero. Repetitions and both signs of a variable are allowed. All lists must be complete and consume the entire input.

For a valid formula \(F\), \(n(F)\) counts its distinct variables and \(N(F)\) counts every encoded bit. On every valid formula, the uniform deterministic multitape machine must halt and decide satisfiability exactly. On malformed strings it must reject in time polynomial in their bit length. The running-time bound on valid formulas is the one in the display below. At each fixed \(q\), define \(s_q\) as the infimum of the \(\alpha\ge0\) for which some such machine and constants \(C\ge1\), \(d\in\mathbb N_0\) satisfy
\[t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(N(F)+1)^d\]
on every valid input. Testing all assignments shows \(0\le s_q\le1\). The machine and constants may depend on \(q,\alpha\). ETH concerns \(s_3\) and SETH concerns the limiting behavior as \(q\) grows.

entries.title: Certified numerical answers and infimum exponents
entries.text:
When a card asks for a numerical value \(x\) to absolute error \(\delta\), an answer \(a\) must come with a proof of \(|a-x|\le\delta\). One way is to prove \(\ell\le x\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le2\delta\), then take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). The answer must specify its value independently of the optimization, limit or unknown quantity the card asks to determine. For a function on a domain \(D\), supply one description of a function \(g\) and prove \(|g(t)-x(t)|\le\delta\) for every \(t\in D\). Two described bounding functions of pointwise width at most \(2\delta\) give such a \(g\) by their midpoint. An exact expression also qualifies. Each card specifies its own precision, any restriction on answer values, and its proof requirements. An interval may enclose an infimum or supremum even when no feasible object attains it.

For a growth exponent defined by \(x=\inf\{a:f(n)=O(n^a)\}\), the implicit constant and the threshold must obey the card’s uniformity requirements. The definition alone supplies neither an \(O(n^x)\) bound at the endpoint nor a limit for \(\log f(n)/\log n\).

entries.title: Synchronous LOCAL and CONGEST rounds
entries.text:
The communication network is a graph. Nodes run a distributed algorithm in synchronous rounds, exchanging messages with their neighbors. LOCAL permits arbitrarily long finite messages. CONGEST bounds the number of bits sent along each edge in each direction per round, typically by \(O(\log n)\) for \(n\) nodes. Local computation is unrestricted between rounds when the card specifies that convention.

The initial information, identifiers, shared or private randomness, and per-node outputs belong to the particular problem. A high-probability guarantee can concern one node or simultaneous correctness of all outputs. The statement specifies which event and which randomness the probability concerns.

cards.title: P versus NP
cards.formal: Does every language in \(\mathrm{NP}\) belong to \(\mathrm{P}\)? Equivalently, is there a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and fixed constants \(C,k\ge1\) such that \(A\) decides SAT on every input of \(N\) bits in at most \(C(N+1)^k\) steps?
cards.definitions: Use the shared definitions of [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np), [SAT](definitions.html#sat) and [uniform bit computation](definitions.html#bit-model). Here \(N\) is the complete bit length of the input formula, including its tree structure, variable identifiers and delimiters. Fix an ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas over AND, OR and NOT, and reject malformed strings. Polynomially interconvertible ordinary encodings give the same P-versus-NP question; this does not assert an unchanged polynomial exponent under every encoding. No oracle, advice or random error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the deterministic uniform model defined here. Equality requires that every NP language have a polynomial-time decision algorithm; inequality requires that at least one NP language have none.
cards.why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.

cards.context:
A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.

NP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.

The two possible answers have different practical limits. \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.

Many successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. These results do not decide P versus NP.

cards.status_note: The Clay Mathematics Institute lists P versus NP as unsolved, checked on 11 September 2026. The cited restricted-circuit lower bounds and proof-method barriers do not resolve the uniform decision problem.

progress.text: The Cook–Levin completeness theorem identifies Boolean satisfiability as NP-complete; Karp reductions connect it to many standard combinatorial problems. This establishes equivalent targets, rather than a separation.

Relativization and subsequent natural-proofs and algebrization barriers delimit broad approaches to separation. The natural-proofs obstruction to general circuit lower bounds is conditional on sufficiently strong pseudorandomness assumptions.

Williams proves that NEXP is not contained in polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits, using faster satisfiability algorithms to obtain lower bounds. ACC has constant depth and modular counting gates. Both the larger language class and the restricted circuit model matter; this does not prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).
The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list P versus NP among its unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

The target concerns worst-case polynomial time on arbitrarily large inputs.

cards.title: Superlinear Boolean circuit lower bounds
cards.formal:
Does there exist one total, length-preserving, deterministic polynomial-time function
\[F:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad |F(x)|=|x|,\]
whose unrestricted Boolean circuit complexity is not linear? Precisely, writing \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{n}\) for its restriction to inputs of length \(n\), the requested lower bound is
\[\forall C>0\ \forall n_0\ge1\ \exists n\ge n_0:\quad \operatorname{CC}_{B_2}(F_n)>Cn.\]
Here \(C\) is real and \(n_0,n\) are integers. The same uniform algorithm computes all \(n\) outputs of \(F_n\) at every length. The lower bound need only exceed every fixed linear bound at arbitrarily large lengths.
cards.definitions:
Length preservation requires exactly \(n\) output bits on an \(n\)-bit input, including the empty output on the empty input. Use the [uniform bit model](definitions.html#bit-model). One deterministic multitape machine computes \(F(x)\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps for a fixed real \(a\ge1\) and integer \(d\ge1\), including the time to write the output.

Use the [Boolean circuit convention](definitions.html#boolean-circuits) with the full \(B_2\) basis and free constants. The circuit has \(n\) inputs and \(n\) ordered output wires, with unrestricted fan-out, sharing and depth. All outputs are computed jointly; an output may directly select an input or constant. Each operation gate, including a unary gate, costs one.

The circuit computes \(F_n\) exactly if its ordered output vector equals \(F_n(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). The number \(\operatorname{CC}_{B_2}(F_n)\) is the minimum gate count of any such circuit. Competing circuits are nonuniform: the choice at each length is independent, and no algorithm is required to construct their descriptions. In contrast, the polynomial-time algorithm for \(F\) must work uniformly at all lengths. This distinction is part of the target.

The statement \(\operatorname{CC}_{B_2}(F_n)=O(n)\) means that there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(n_0\ge1\) such that \(\operatorname{CC}_{B_2}(F_n)\le Cn\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\). The displayed target is its exact negation. It does not require \(\operatorname{CC}_{B_2}(F_n)/n\) to tend to infinity at every sufficiently large length. The function, its program and its running-time polynomial are chosen before all the lower-bound quantifiers.

The source uses AND, OR and NOT gates and leaves “explicit” broad. Every full-basis gate has a constant-size AND/OR/NOT implementation, and those gates are already allowed in \(B_2\). Thus changing between these two fixed bases changes minimum size by at most a constant factor and preserves the not-\(O(n)\) target. The polynomial-time explicitness convention is the previously recorded specialization of the source; it is not claimed to be equivalent to every possible meaning of “explicit.” No linearity or other algebraic restriction is imposed on \(F\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated existence claim. A positive answer must specify one total length-preserving function, prove that one uniform deterministic algorithm computes it in polynomial time, and prove the displayed lower bound against every circuit in the full model. A negative answer must show that every such polynomial-time function has \(O(n)\)-size nonuniform circuits, allowing the constant and starting length to depend on the function. A fixed constant-factor lower bound does not establish the target. Nor does a lower bound only for formulas, monotone circuits, XOR-only circuits or a fixed depth bound without a proof extending it to unrestricted circuits. The claim is unconditional, and an oracle-relative or conditional separation alone does not settle it. All complexity and quantifier requirements are exact; no numerical acceptance tolerance applies.
cards.why: A superlinear lower bound would establish a basic limitation on unrestricted nonuniform computation for an efficiently computable function. It would surpass every fixed linear gate count, even when a circuit can reuse work freely across outputs, and expose structure that simple counting does not identify.

cards.context:
A circuit may reuse any intermediate result and share it among different outputs. Those permissions make it stronger than a formula, whose computation is organized as a tree. The question retains all this circuit power and asks for an efficiently computable function that cannot be implemented with a fixed number of gates per input bit.

Counting proves that most Boolean truth tables require exponentially many gates. It does not supply a function computable by one polynomial-time algorithm, so it does not satisfy this card’s explicitness requirement. The challenge is obtaining a size lower bound for a computationally accessible function.

Linear maps over \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\), with addition modulo two, form a significant special case. An efficiently constructible binary matrix \(A_n\) defines \(F_n(x)=A_nx\). Counting gives matrices needing \(\Omega(n^2/\log n)\) gates, but the 2026 source still identifies a superlinear lower bound for explicit matrices as open. A lower bound for circuits using only XOR gates would not automatically apply to circuits with arbitrary Boolean gates.

The desired function already has polynomial-size circuits because its uniform polynomial-time computation can be simulated by circuits. The question therefore separates linear size from polynomial size within efficient computation. Such a lower bound alone is not a proof that \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Conversely, a hard NP language need not be polynomial-time computable and so need not meet this card’s explicitness condition.

Li and Yang prove a \(3.1n-o(n)\) lower bound for suitable affine dispersers in the full two-input Boolean basis. An affine disperser is nonconstant on every affine subspace above its specified dimension threshold; suitable examples are polynomial-time computable. This is a substantial improvement of the known linear constant, while every fixed constant remains compatible with \(O(n)\) circuits.

The 2025 covering paper relates circuit lower bounds to combinatorial cover complexity and proves bounds for random graphs. Its results do not exhibit a polynomial-time function with the superlinear unrestricted circuit lower bound requested here.

The February 2026 gate-elimination preprint gives formal simplification results for selected bases and an efficiently checkable form of a classical linear parity lower bound. Its additional proof structure does not supply a superlinear unrestricted bound.

Raz’s July 2026 revision proves conditional barriers for matrix natural proofs: proofs identifying a sufficiently large set of hard matrices recognizable in time polynomial in the matrix description. Under the cryptographic assumptions stated in that paper, pseudorandom matrices with small circuits obstruct this defined proof class. The near-linear and linear circuit-size barriers rely on different assumptions; neither rules out all possible proofs of this card’s target.

cards.title: L versus NL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\)? Equivalently, do there exist a single deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and a constant \(C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), directed graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(s,t\in[n]\), the machine halts, correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), and visits at most
\[C\left\lceil\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil\]
work-tape cells? The graph is given explicitly by its adjacency matrix; the input is read-only. The machine and constant must work for all input sizes.
cards.definitions:
A directed graph has a set \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\) of ordered edges. Self-loops are allowed. Reachability asks whether there are vertices \(v_0=s,\ldots,v_\ell=t\), with \(\ell\ge0\), such that \((v_{i-1},v_i)\in E\) for every \(1\le i\le\ell\). In particular \(s=t\) is a yes instance. No degree, planarity, acyclicity or unique-path restriction is imposed.

The input contains a self-delimiting binary encoding of \(n\), all \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, and \(s,t\) in fixed-length binary vertex fields. Its bit length is \(N=\Theta(n^2)\), so logarithmic bounds in \(N+2\) and \(n+2\) agree up to constants. Malformed strings, including invalid dimensions and vertex fields, are rejected with logarithmic workspace in their actual length. A validity check does not need to store the matrix. The representation is an explicit string, not an adjacency oracle or a circuit describing a much larger graph.

The computation uses a fixed finite program, a read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. Heads move by ordinary Turing-machine steps. Space is the total number of distinct work-tape cells visited during the computation, including blank cells crossed by heads, all counters, stacks and auxiliary records. The finite control and read-only input cells are uncharged. There is no advice depending on input size, oracle, random tape, external storage, writable input or extra tape whose contents can temporarily be borrowed. The output is a single accept/reject decision. Input rescanning and arbitrary finite computation are permitted, but every input must eventually halt.

Use [L and NL](definitions.html#space) with the read-only input and work-space convention above. A nondeterministic branch may be clocked in polynomial time because the number of logspace configurations is polynomial.

Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions. Such a reduction writes one polynomial-length instance and preserves its yes/no answer while using logarithmic workspace; output bits can be recomputed when composing it with another small-space machine. Thus a positive answer for the specified matrix representation implies \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{L}\), and \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\) already holds.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\), using the stated uniform machine model. An affirmative reachability solution must specify one machine and a constant, and prove correctness, termination, malformed-input handling and the space bound on every input. A negative solution must exclude every such machine: equivalently, for every always-halting correct deterministic reachability decider and every constant \(C\), some valid instance exceeds \(C\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) visited work cells. A class-based argument must establish the equivalence to this concrete reachability target. A lower bound for one search procedure, or a successful algorithm restricted to undirected graphs, using advice, nondeterminism or a higher power of logarithmic space, is insufficient. No numerical approximation of a resource bound answers this exact class-equality question.
cards.why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.

cards.context:
Ordinary graph search can remember which vertices have been visited. Logarithmic space holds only a constant number of vertex names and counters, so a separate visited bit for each vertex does not fit. Repeated scans of the input are free of a space penalty, but any saved information between scans counts.

Directed reachability captures an entire complexity class because a small-space machine has only polynomially many configurations. Its legal next steps form the edges of a directed graph, and acceptance is reachability of an accepting configuration. This correspondence is computable with logarithmic workspace.

Savitch’s theorem gives deterministic reachability using \(O((\log n)^2)\) workspace, with a quasipolynomial time bound. The gap between one and two logarithmic factors is exactly relevant to membership in L: an always-halting deterministic machine using only logarithmic space has polynomially many configurations, and hence polynomial running time.

Reingold’s theorem meets the logarithmic-space target when edges are undirected. Directed graphs therefore cannot be replaced by their undirected versions: forgetting an arrow can create paths absent from the original instance.

The equality \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) means that nondeterministic logarithmic space can recognize both reachability and nonreachability. It is a closure theorem within the nondeterministic model, and does not establish that either task has a deterministic logarithmic-space algorithm.

The 2025 alternative links graph connectivity to random-walk estimation, but its successful procedure may differ from graph to graph. Its deterministic branch uses polylogarithmic rather than logarithmic space. Neither qualification disappears merely because both algorithms signal their own failures.

The 2026 hardness result locates the difficulty even in graphs whose edges split into two sets, each a collection of directed paths of length at most two. This remains NL-hard when the decomposition is part of the input. The pieces are simple, but paths using edges from both pieces can still express general directed reachability.

Savitch’s and Immerman’s original publisher abstracts, Reingold’s author manuscript introduction, the 2025 author version’s Theorem 1, and the 2026 publisher abstract/introduction/Theorem 3.1 statement support the recorded progress. progress.text: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in \(O(s^{2})\) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-space algorithm.

Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\), so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms.
Reingold obtains deterministic logarithmic space for undirected connectivity, published at STOC 2005 and subsequently in JACM. Arbitrary directed graphs are outside that theorem.

Doron, Pyne, Tell and Williams give two fixed algorithms with a per-graph guarantee: at least one succeeds, either solving directed reachability in deterministic polynomial time and polylogarithmic space, or estimating length-n random-walk probabilities in nondeterministic logarithmic space. Both report failure and always respect their resource bounds. This alternative does not provide a deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm on all graphs.

Bhadra and Tewari show NL-hardness even for directed graphs whose edges can be partitioned into two forests of directed paths of length at most two, including when the partition is supplied. Such a simple decomposition therefore does not make the general logspace obstacle disappear.

sentences: Directed reachability asks whether a path follows the arrows from a specified source to a target.
Nondeterministic logarithmic space can recognize it, and the problem captures the whole class NL.
The target is one always-correct deterministic algorithm with only logarithmic writable memory on every explicit input.
Savitch’s larger-space simulation and Reingold’s undirected algorithm do not settle this directed logarithmic-space target.
A solution requires either a uniform algorithm with all resource guarantees or a lower bound excluding every eligible deterministic decider.

cards.title: P versus PSPACE
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? Equivalently, can a single deterministic Turing machine decide the truth of every fully quantified Boolean formula in \(C(N+1)^k\) steps for fixed \(C,k\ge1\), where \(N\) is its encoded bit length?
cards.definitions: Use [P](definitions.html#p-np), [PSPACE](definitions.html#space) and [TQBF](definitions.html#polynomial-hierarchy). Each well-formed input gives an explicit quantifier prefix on distinct Boolean variables followed by an AND/OR/NOT formula whose variables are all bound. Its full binary encoding, including variable identifiers, counts toward \(N\). Reject malformed inputs. The number of quantifiers and alternations may grow with the instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\). The first outcome asserts a deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure for every polynomial-space language; the second asserts a polynomial-space language with no deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure.
cards.why: This asks whether reusing a feasible amount of memory can provide computational power beyond feasible running time. It is a central unresolved separation even when the allowed language class is enlarged from NP to all of PSPACE, and it organizes the complexity of quantified reasoning, games, and verification.

cards.context:
Time measures the total number of computation steps; space measures how much information the machine retains at once. Space can be reused. For example, a machine can evaluate a quantified formula by recursively exploring possible choices and reusing its work area when it returns from a branch. The resulting computation may inspect exponentially many choices while keeping only a polynomial amount of information.

Alternating quantifiers express a finite game of choices: existential moves try to make the final formula true, and universal moves challenge them. For example, \(\forall x\exists y (y=x)\) is true because y may depend on x, whereas \(\exists y\forall x (y=x)\) is false. Both variables range over \(\{0,1\}\). A winning strategy for a longer formula can have exponentially many branches even though each play has polynomial length. Polynomial-time alternation captures exactly PSPACE.

The inclusion \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\) is immediate, but its strictness is unknown. \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) would imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\) because \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\). A proof of \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), however, would collapse the polynomial hierarchy without automatically giving a polynomial-time algorithm for formulas with an unbounded number of quantifier alternations. This separates the present question from merely solving satisfiability.

The theorem \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) characterizes the same space class through interaction: a polynomial-time randomized verifier can check claims from an unbounded prover using a bounded-error interactive protocol. The prover’s assistance is a resource. Removing the prover to obtain an ordinary deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is not a consequence of that characterization.

Williams’ time-to-space simulation gives a concrete advance in the comparison of these resources. For time bounds \(t(n)\ge n, a\) time-t multitape computation can be simulated in \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) working space. A consequence is that some linear-space languages require time \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) for every \(\varepsilon >0\). The lower-bound exponent remains bounded: the result does not exhibit a polynomial-space language outside every polynomial time bound.

cards.title: Minimum Circuit Size Problem
cards.formal:
Is the Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP), with a complete truth table as input, NP-complete under uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time function \(g\) such that
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad x\in\mathrm{SAT}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g(x)\in\mathrm{MCSP}?\]
Use the exact circuit model and language below. The target is unconditional and unrelativized. A reduction may not use random bits, advice, an oracle, a gap promise, a partial truth table or an implicitly represented truth table.
cards.definitions:
Use the [Boolean circuit convention](definitions.html#boolean-circuits) \(\mathrm{DM}\): binary AND/OR and unary NOT, with one output and free input wires, constant sources and wires. Every operation gate, including NOT, counts. The minimum size is \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\). This is the source's total-gate \(R\) measure; it is not a binary-gate-only measure or the full \(B_2\) basis. Exact thresholds below use this convention.

The truth table \(t\in\{0,1\}^{N}\), where \(N=2^n\), lists the values of a total function \(f_t:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) in lexicographic input order. A well-formed instance is \((t,s)\), with integer \(0\le s\le N\) written in binary. It is a yes-instance exactly when \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_t)\le s\). To fix a binary language, encode a pair as \(1^{|t|}0t\operatorname{bin}(s)\), with no leading zeros in \(\operatorname{bin}(s)\), except that zero is encoded as the single bit 0. Strings failing this syntax, the power-of-two length requirement, \(n\ge1\), or the threshold bound are no-instances. The input length is \(2N+1+O(\log(N+1))\), so polynomial time is measured in the full truth-table length, not merely in the number \(n\) of variables. The redundant unary length prefix is only a fixed efficiently decodable pair encoding.

Constants have been made explicit to remove a convention left implicit in the source. For a nonconstant function, constant inputs can be eliminated gate by gate without increasing size, so allowing them does not change its optimum. For the two constant functions the answer follows directly from the specified convention. No claim that all Boolean bases preserve exact optimum sizes is needed.

Use the shared definitions of [polynomial-time many-one reductions](definitions.html#reductions) and [SAT](definitions.html#sat), with uniform deterministic bit computation and one explicitly written target instance. SAT uses a fixed ordinary explicit binary formula encoding, with malformed inputs rejected. Polynomially interconvertible ordinary formula encodings preserve this reduction question.

Use [NP](definitions.html#p-np) and [NP-hardness and completeness](definitions.html#reductions) in their shared senses. MCSP is in NP: a circuit with at most \(s\le N\) gates has an explicit topologically ordered description of \(O(N\log(N+1))\) bits, and evaluating it on all \(N\) assignments checks the entire table in polynomial time. Thus the displayed SAT reduction suffices, by SAT's NP-completeness, and its nonexistence would refute NP-completeness under this reduction convention.

For context only, use the shared definitions of [P](definitions.html#p-np) and [BPP](definitions.html#randomization). The source also asks whether MCSP might lie in BPP. That is a separate proposition, not the logical negation of NP-hardness: the two possibilities are not an unconditional exhaustive or disjoint classification.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the displayed SAT-to-MCSP reduction. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic reduction, prove its polynomial running time and output length, and prove the yes/no equivalence for every input using the exact total truth-table and gate-count conventions above. A negative answer must prove that every deterministic polynomial-time candidate reduction fails on some input. A conditional theorem, an oracle-relative theorem, hardness under randomized or quasipolynomial-time reductions, a lower bound for a restricted proof system, or hardness of a partial, implicit or gap variant does not alone meet this criterion. No additive numerical tolerance applies to this exact language-reduction statement.
cards.why: MCSP asks how hard it is to recognize computational simplicity from complete data. Its classification connects NP-completeness with circuit lower bounds, learning and cryptography. A proof or refutation of standard NP-hardness would settle a central question about whether circuit minimization has the same reduction-based difficulty as general NP search.

cards.context:
MCSP asks whether a fully specified Boolean function has a short circuit. Finding a short representation is an optimization task; this decision version asks whether a proposed size threshold can be met. Its input already contains every function value, which makes checking a proposed circuit efficient.

The main target is the NP-hardness question shared by the three source passages consolidated into this card. The original primary passage also raises membership in BPP. That broader classification is retained here as context rather than being silently identified with the negation of NP-hardness.

The circuit basis matters for exact minimization. The 2026 source treats both counting all gates and counting only binary gates; this card explicitly uses its total-gate convention. The source continues to identify ordinary MCSP hardness as open and distinguishes it from successful hardness results for partial specifications.

Austrin and Risse establish strong lower bounds for sum-of-squares refutations of formulas asserting that a small circuit exists. Sum-of-squares is a particular algebraic proof system. Its limitations give information about a restricted method of certifying circuit lower bounds, without proving that every efficient algorithm for ordinary MCSP fails.

Hirahara and Ilango obtain deterministic quasipolynomial-time nonadaptive hardness, including constant-factor approximation, under three assumptions together: subexponentially secure noninteractive witness-indistinguishable proofs for SAT, almost-everywhere subexponential nondeterministic circuit lower bounds for coNP, and almost-everywhere near-maximum circuit lower bounds for \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{NP}}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here nonadaptive means that a reduction prepares all oracle questions before receiving answers. Both its assumptions and its longer running time distinguish this result from the target.

The June 2026 ECCC manuscript studies an implicit version whose function is represented by a circuit sampling labeled examples, rather than by the full table. Its randomized gap-hardness result assumes subexponential versions of indistinguishability obfuscation and the nonexistence of an optimal propositional proof system. This is further progress on a related representation, not an unconditional many-one reduction to the language defined here.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm{P}\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.
cards.why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

cards.context:
The same graph can appear under many vertex names. For example, renumbering a cycle leaves its adjacency relations unchanged as an unlabeled structure. Isomorphism asks whether this explains the entire difference between two inputs. A proposed bijection can be checked efficiently, but a negative instance requires ruling out all bijections. This places the decision problem in NP, the class with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time.

Simple summaries can agree on different graphs: a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices and every vertex has degree two. They are not isomorphic because one is connected and the other is disconnected. Any complete decision procedure must distinguish every nonisomorphic pair, including pairs with much stronger coincident invariants.

Babai’s general upper bound has the form \(\exp((\log(n+2))^{O(1)})\). This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, whose permitted exponents go beyond the fixed polynomial bound requested here. It does not prove a superpolynomial lower bound on the problem or on every implementation of that method.

Efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes provide substantial structure without settling the unrestricted target. In particular, a runtime with a degree or width parameter in the exponent is polynomial when that parameter is fixed, but it need not be polynomial when the parameter grows with the input. The 2026 survey explicitly separates these parameterized bounds from the general open problem.

A randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error for ordinary isomorphism would settle the neighboring BPP question. It would not by itself provide the deterministic algorithm asked for here. A quantum algorithm deciding the same ordinary relation is another computational variant; the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism is a different mathematical target.

The two consolidated MFCS 2021 sources independently restate the general polynomial-time question. Butti and Dalmau discuss it beside fractional homomorphisms and linear-programming relaxations. Dawar and Vagnozzi discuss its equivalence to computing automorphism-orbit partitions and compare algebraic relaxations. These source contexts are preserved without substituting a conjecture about one relaxation for general graph isomorphism.

The author correction and both consolidated primary-source passages were checked. Targeted subsequent searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified general polynomial-time result; this bounded search and formulation audit do not independently verify every cited proof.

progress.text: Babai announces the general quasipolynomial-time isomorphism algorithm and presents the result at STOC 2016. The available arXiv versions predate the later correction.

Babai reports a replacement for the recursive call whose analysis had invalidated the original runtime claim, restoring quasipolynomial time. The January 14 addition supplies the corrected recursive step.
Babai’s ICM survey records the corrected general frontier and the unresolved possibility of polynomial time.

Neuen’s published survey explicitly describes general graph isomorphism as neither known to be polynomial-time solvable nor known to be NP-complete. Its newer upper bounds concern specified graph parameters.

sentences: Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite simple graphs agree after a bijective relabeling of their vertices.
The target is a single deterministic algorithm that answers correctly on every explicitly encoded pair in polynomial time.
A proposed relabeling is easy to verify, while ruling out all relabelings can require substantially more structure.
The checked general upper bound is quasipolynomial, and efficient algorithms for restricted graph classes do not establish the unrestricted polynomial bound.
A resolution would settle a central structural comparison problem whose position between P and NP-completeness remains unresolved.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order. Each entry has a presence flag and, when present, one exact finite real weight. Thus there is at most one edge for each ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges have no weight and are represented by the flag, not by a large finite number. There is no bound on the magnitude, sign or precision of a real weight. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle of negative total weight, including negative self-loops.

A finite directed walk \((v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) has weight \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})\). The empty walk from a vertex to itself has weight zero. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\), the distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or the separate symbol \(+\infty\) if none exists. The no-negative-cycle promise ensures that every reachable minimum is finite and attained; nonnegative cycles can be removed, so a simple path suffices for distinct endpoints. In particular \(d_G(u,u)=0\). Zero-weight cycles and equal shortest distances are allowed. Output consists of all \(n^2\) exact distances in vertex-pair order, each a real value or an unreachable flag. Printing the vertices of every shortest path is not required.

The machine has one fixed finite program and two kinds of random-access memory cell: exact real cells and finite index-word cells. One real-cell load, store or copy, addition, subtraction, or comparison costs one step; comparison returns its trichotomy result as a word. These are the only operations inspecting real values. Real constants built into the finite program are restricted to \(0\) and \(1\); there are no arbitrary advice constants. A real value cannot be converted to its digits, an integer address, or its floor. Multiplication or division of real cells and operations packing several arbitrary reals into one word are not available.

For some fixed integer \(a\ge4\) chosen as part of the program's model, an index word has \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Word loads, stores, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) cost one step. Unsigned integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step; division by zero is an invalid computation. A shift of at least \(b(n)\) positions returns zero. Addresses are words. All accessed cells must fit in this address range; a new work cell starts at zero and each access is charged. Word operations can process indices, counters and comparison results; they do not reveal the representation of a real edge weight. The input matrix and initially empty work memory are the only input-dependent initial state.

The randomized instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit per step. All preprocessing, table construction, memory access, random-bit generation, input reading and output writing are charged to the same runtime. There is no nonuniform table supplied for free, extra prediction, oracle, parallel work unit or quantum operation. The bound is worst case over the input and every coin sequence. For each fixed promised graph, the probability that the whole output matrix is correct must be at least \(2/3\); separate success probabilities for individual entries are insufficient. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the coins.

The bound depends on \(n\), not the bit length or magnitude of weights, because the real operations are exact primitives. This is a classical real-operation question, not an ordinary bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real encodings. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1]\) preserves existence of a fixed positive exponent saving; any positive saving implies a smaller such rational saving. No behavior is required on graphs violating the no-negative-cycle promise.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation in this exact machine model. A positive proof must exhibit one finite uniform program and fixed constants, prove the promised-graph distance semantics and joint correctness probability, and charge every operation to the worst-case \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) bound. A negative proof must rule out every such program and every fixed positive exponent saving, including randomized programs.

A result for bounded integer weights, a restricted graph family, approximate distances, a single source, or additional accurate predictions does not settle this target. Neither does a lower bound restricted to one reduction method or to machines lacking the permitted word operations. An unproved APSP hardness hypothesis cannot serve as the proof of its own consequence here. A bound \(n^3/f(n)\) with only a subpolynomial saving \(f(n)=n^{o(1)}\) does not establish a fixed exponent saving; expected running time alone does not establish the specified worst-case bound. There is no additive or multiplicative error allowance in the distance output.
cards.why: All-pairs distances are a basic graph primitive. A fixed improvement over the cubic exponent would also change the complexity of several equivalent path, matrix and weighted-triangle problems. Their reductions make the exact weight and machine assumptions essential to interpreting claimed improvements.
