cards.context:
If the edges from u to v, u to z and z to v have weights 8, 5 and −2, and there are no other edges, then the shortest u-to-v distance is 3. Negative edges are compatible with a finite exact answer. By contrast, a negative cycle reachable on a u-to-v walk would make its weights unbounded below; the input promise excludes that case. An unreachable ordered pair is reported separately from every finite distance.

The corresponding min-plus matrix operation is \((X\star Y)_{ij}=\min_k(X_{ik}+Y_{kj})\). This uses minimum and addition, whereas ordinary matrix multiplication uses addition and multiplication. Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish subcubic equivalences among APSP, min-plus products, negative edge-weighted triangles and related tasks. Their integer-range theorem carries weight-length factors; Section 4.3 separately gives a randomized strongly polynomial reduction whose overhead depends on the matrix dimension instead. These equivalences preserve existence of some positive saving, not necessarily its exact exponent.

Williams gives a randomized real-RAM bound \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), and a deterministic subpolynomial improvement with a different exponent in the denominator. These are substantial savings over cubic time. Nevertheless, for each fixed \(c>0\), the expression \(n^3/2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{3-c/\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) has an exponent tending to three. That bound alone does not establish \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). The algorithms permit ordinary computation on finite words as well as comparisons and additions of weights.

Abboud and coauthors study graphs with at most \(d\) distinct weights on the outgoing edges of each vertex. Their Theorem 1.4 gives a fixed exponent saving when \(d\le n^{3-\omega-\delta}\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(\omega\) is the ordinary matrix-multiplication exponent. This theorem is stated in their bounded-integer word-RAM setting. Theorem 1.2 for one outgoing weight per vertex also has an explicitly stated real-weight extension in Section 4.4. Neither statement covers unrestricted arbitrary real edge weights with up to \(n\) different outgoing weights per vertex.

Akmal and Fischer’s ICALP 2026 Theorem 1 solves zero-sum node-weighted triangle detection in \(O(\mathrm{MM}(n))\) time. Here a triangle’s value is the sum of three vertex weights, and \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\) denotes an admissible running-time bound for ordinary matrix multiplication, with the paper’s monotonicity convention. This is different from independently weighting every edge. The introduction explicitly retains the unresolved fixed-exponent improvement for minimum edge-weighted triangles. The paper uses \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\), rather than asserting that the infimum exponent \(\omega\) must be attained.

Polak and Schmidt’s July 2026 preprint gives an exact APSP algorithm with supplied prediction certificates and running time \(O(n^{2.83}+\eta n)\) for its chosen parameters. The error measure \(\eta\) counts vertex pairs whose induced distance estimates are incorrect or fail the paper’s verification condition. It can be as large as \(n^2\), so this guarantee can still be cubic. Obtaining a sufficiently accurate certificate at no charged cost is an additional input assumption, not a uniform worst-case solution of this card.

Sheffield, Vassilevska Williams and Xi’s August 2026 preprint proves limits on reductions that treat a triangle relation as a black box and must work for every such relation. Its Definition 1 makes this uniformity across relations essential. These limits concern the strength of a particular reduction model, not a lower bound excluding every algorithm for the fixed shortest-path problem.

source_formulation.text: This retains the existing arbitrary-real-weight randomized APSP question and its comparison-addition model with ordinary logarithmic-size word operations. It makes uniformity, primitive operations, the graph promise and joint output guarantee explicit. The cited equivalence literature also states integer-weight theorems with a logarithmic dependence on the weight range; its strongly polynomial reduction is identified separately rather than silently equating all weight and machine conventions.

cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked on 15 September 2026. The published July 2026 node-weighted-triangle introduction and July prediction-assisted APSP preprint explicitly retain the general fixed-exponent challenge. The inspected few-weight algorithms, extra-prediction bounds and August black-box reduction barriers do not resolve the uniform randomized comparison-addition real-RAM question stated here. Bounded current searches located no full matching solution claim. This is an individual formulation and source-scope review, not exhaustive certification of every cited proof or all later literature.

sentences: The input is a directed graph with arbitrary exact real edge weights and no negative cycle, and the output gives the shortest distance for every ordered vertex pair.
The target is one uniform randomized algorithm with a fixed positive saving below the cubic exponent, correct on the entire output matrix with probability at least two thirds.
Time is charged in a specified comparison-addition real RAM that also permits ordinary logarithmic-size word operations, including all preprocessing and output.
Known general algorithms achieve subpolynomial savings, while faster restricted results concern node weights, few outgoing weights, or supplied predictions.
Recent restrictions on black-box reductions do not rule out all APSP algorithms, and the inspected sources retain the full target as unresolved.

problem_origin.note: The cubic APSP barrier dates to the Floyd–Warshall era in 1962. A fixed polynomial improvement is the later standard formulation of that longstanding speedup question; the modern fine-grained conjecture is newer.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
cards.why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

references.title: Integer models of computation and integer sorting
references.locator: Spring 2025, Lecture 3; word-RAM model and slide 26 explicit open question

cards.context:
Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles \(w=O(\log  n)\). Divide each key into digits of about \(\log _{2}n\) bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size \(O(n)\). There are \(O(1+w/\log  n)\) passes, giving \(O(n(1+w/\log  n))\) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If \(w=(\log  n)^{3/2}\), however, that same argument takes about \(\sqrt{\log  n}\) passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’\(s O(n\sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic \(O(n \log  \log  n)\) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.

The question asks for one always-correct randomized word-RAM algorithm taking expected linear time for every permitted word length.

This tests whether powerful word operations can completely remove the asymptotic overhead of ordering an arbitrary list of machine words.

cards.title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
cards.formal:
Does exact symmetric weighted travelling salesman admit a classical algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two, allowing bounded-error randomization and polynomial dependence on the input bit length?

Precisely, do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), positive integers \(K,c,B\) with \(B\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(\mathcal A\) such that, for every \(n\ge3\) and every complete undirected graph on vertices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with nonnegative integer edge weights encoded as below, both of the following hold?
\[\Pr[\mathcal A\text{ outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle}]\ge\frac23,\]
\[\text{number of charged operations on every random execution}\ \le\ K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+N)^c.\]
Here \(N\) is the total bit length of the explicit input, and the machine model is fixed below using \(B\). All constants and the algorithm precede the quantifiers over the graph, its weights and its encoding length. A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.
cards.definitions:
Instance and encoding. There is one weight \(a_{ij}=a_{ji}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for each unordered pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), and no loops. Weights are exact integers of arbitrary finite bit length. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\). Define the self-delimiting code
\[U(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t).\]
The input is \(U(n)\) followed by \(U(a_{ij})\) in lexicographic order of \((i,j)\), for all \(1\le i<j\le n\). Its length in bits is \(N\). No matrix entry is supplied implicitly by an oracle or by a succinct circuit.

Objective and output. A tour is any permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), interpreted cyclically. Set \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\). Its cost and the optimum are
\[\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{\pi(i),\pi(i+1)},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(a)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi),\]
where \(S_n\) is the finite set of all such permutations. The graph is complete, so a tour always exists and the minimum is attained. The output is the explicit list of its \(n\) vertex labels, each in \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Any minimum-cost tour is accepted, including any rotation or reversal of one; no uniqueness is required. An invalid list, an explicit failure output, or a suboptimal tour counts as failure. Returning only the optimum value, a bound or an approximate tour is not the required output.

Machine and charges. Use a word RAM whose word length on this input is
\[w=B\left\lceil n+\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil\text{ bits}.\]
The algorithm has one finite program independent of \(n,N\) and all weights. A word is an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); a memory address is one word. The input bits are packed in order into consecutive read-only words, padding the last word with zeros and exposing the true input length. Working memory is initially zero and contains no advice or precomputed tables. Reading or writing one addressed word, copying a word, comparing two words, branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and a left or right shift by a word-specified amount each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Addition, subtraction and multiplication are modulo \(2^w\) and cost one operation; integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one operation. Division by zero is not permitted. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one operation. Outputting a word, including the final partial word, costs one operation.

Integers longer than one word must be represented and processed using multiple charged operations; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers or exact real numbers. Reading and decoding the input, constructing tables, generating random bits, preprocessing, arithmetic and writing the entire tour are included in the clock. Addressing exponential-size subset tables is allowed by the linear-in-\(n\) word length. There is no separate polynomial-space restriction, and no quantum memory, quantum query, advice string or ideal oracle. The fixed polynomial overhead permitted in \(n+N\) accommodates the bit cost of operations on these finite-width words; this does not assert that sequential simulation of arbitrary random memory access has only polynomial overhead.

Probability and uniformity. For each fixed input the probability is over the machine’s independent fair coin stream. The same success guarantee holds on every input, not just on average over a distribution of weights. The running-time bound holds for every possible coin stream, including unsuccessful executions, so it is a worst-case clock rather than an expected-time bound. The constants \(\varepsilon,K,c,B\) cannot depend on the weights, their range or any property of the instance.

Scope. There is no triangle inequality, Euclidean geometry, bounded-weight, small-doubling or other structural promise. Polynomial dependence on \(N\) is allowed; polynomial dependence on the numerical maximum or sum of the weights is not automatically allowed. The fixed saving \(\varepsilon>0\) cannot tend to zero with \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation. A positive proof must specify one uniform classical algorithm and fixed constants, prove the worst-case clock including input and output costs, and prove per-instance success probability at least \(2/3\) for an exactly optimal tour. A negative proof must exclude every such algorithm and every permitted choice of constants in the stated randomized word-RAM model. A conditional lower bound settles only that conditional assertion. A restriction on one dynamic-programming framework, a local-search rule or a polynomial-space algorithm does not exclude all allowed algorithms. Faster Hamiltonicity detection, pseudo-polynomial dependence on weight magnitudes, a restricted weight class, approximate optimization or a quantum algorithm does not meet the full positive target.
cards.why: Exact weighted TSP is a basic test of whether optimization over all orders of a set fundamentally requires base-two exponential time. A fixed reduction of that base would save an exponential factor for every sufficiently large instance, even when costs have arbitrary binary representations. Understanding this boundary would distinguish the difficulty of selecting an optimal tour from the already faster task of merely detecting a tour.

cards.context:
In a complete graph the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle is automatic. The difficulty is selecting the cheapest one among the possible orders. Two tours with almost identical edges can have very different costs, and there is no restriction tying those costs to a geometric distance. The card therefore concerns exact optimization rather than finding any spanning cycle.

The Bellman and Held–Karp algorithms from 1962 give the familiar \(O(2^n n^2)\) arithmetic-operation bound. Stoian’s 2024 result improves this to deterministic time \(2^n n^2/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) in its stated model. This is a real improvement to the long-standing bound, but its exponent is still \(n-o(n)\). It does not give a fixed constant \(\varepsilon>0\) in \((2-\varepsilon)^n\). Arbitrary-length costs still require the bit-length accounting stated in this card.

Björklund gives a Monte Carlo \(O^*(1.657^n)\) algorithm for undirected Hamiltonicity. The weighted extension in Theorem 3 has running time \(O^*(W1.657^n)\), where \(W\) is the sum of the positive integer edge weights. A value \(2^b\) needs only \(b+1\) binary digits, so a factor polynomial in \(W\) can be exponential in the number of input bits used for weights. That extension does not establish the arbitrary-binary-weight target.

The input-bit distinction is not a demand for strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. A polynomial factor in the total binary encoding length is expressly allowed. What is excluded is hiding dependence on enormous numerical weights inside that factor. Likewise, randomized success must hold on each fixed instance, and every execution must obey the clock. A favorable average over sampled instances is a different guarantee.

The STACS 2026 small-doubling result goes beyond numerically small weights. If \(A\) is the set of distinct input weights and \(A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}\), its promise is \(|A+A|\le C|A|\) for a fixed constant \(C\). Under that additional structure, the stated TSP time matches the unweighted exponential scale, with factors depending on \(C\). Arbitrary weight sets need not have a bounded doubling constant; allowing \(C\) to grow with the input does not give this card’s fixed uniform bound.

Time and memory are separate resources. Dallant and Kozma’s April 2026 paper improves interior time-space tradeoffs: it studies running time \(T^{n+o(n)}\) and space \(S^{n+o(n)}\) for \(2<T<4\), obtaining a product \(ST<3.572\) at one point. An improvement in the product does not assert \(T<2\). The paper explicitly retains the base-two running-time question as open.

The July 2026 follow-up improves the achievable time-space product to roughly \(3.1819\) in the relevant set-system framework. Its lower bound of more than \(3.1818\) is a limitation of that framework, whose parameters describe families of subsets and their chains. It is not a lower bound against arbitrary randomized TSP algorithms. The introduction still identifies \(O^*(2^n)\) as the best known unrestricted classical time scale.

Quantum algorithms form a different comparison. Dallant’s July 2026 theorem assumes quantum computation and quantum random-access memory. The saving from quantum search cannot be treated as an implementation on a classical RAM with independent random bits. The selected target permits classical randomization but supplies no quantum operations.

The ESA paper published on 25 August 2026 similarly reports a time base of 1.859 with a QRAM space base of 1.315. The inspected official abstract makes the quantum resource explicit. Those sub-two numbers therefore do not constitute a classical solution to this card; the full theorem was not independently audited in this review.

The SODA 2026 paper on \(k\)-opt proves that prescribed local-improvement processes can take exponentially many iterations even with an optimal choice of improving move. Its conclusion concerns those processes, including particular three- and four-edge neighborhoods. The card allows all uniform algorithms, and asks for a global optimum, so that lower bound is not the logical negation of the target.

The question also imposes no polynomial-space requirement. An exponential-space algorithm with a fixed time base below two would qualify. Limits on a specific time-space curve, a subset recurrence or a local search rule do not establish an unrestricted impossibility theorem. The reviewed sources distinguish this open algorithmic question from a conjectured hardness assumption for another problem.

source_formulation.text: Preserves importance 96 and the existing editorial choice of complete symmetric TSP with arbitrary nonnegative binary integer weights, bounded-error classical randomization, a worst-case clock and polynomial bit-length overhead. Retains the random-access model with word length proportional to n+log(L), so the statement does not silently replace exponential-space random access by a slower sequential machine. Stoian’s 2024 question concerns the prefactor of the historical bound; the broader fixed-base question is explicitly discussed as open in Dallant–Kozma and the July 2026 follow-up.

No fixed-base classical algorithm with polynomial dependence solely on arbitrary input bit length was found in the bounded search; abstract-only checks and proof-review limits are recorded separately.

sentences: Exact weighted TSP asks for a cheapest tour through every vertex of a complete undirected graph.
This question seeks a uniform classical algorithm with a fixed exponential time base below two.
Weights are arbitrary nonnegative integers written in binary, and only polynomial dependence on their total encoding length is allowed.
Bounded-error randomization and exponential memory are permitted, but every execution must satisfy the stated worst-case clock.
Recent prefactor, structured-weight, time-space and quantum improvements do not establish the full classical guarantee.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic comparison-RAM algorithm that, for every finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with arbitrary real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(n+m)\) worst-case total time, where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\)? The graph is explicitly listed, and weights are opaque keys that may only be copied and compared. The machine, output and quantifier conventions are fixed below; the bound counts all computation, not only weight comparisons.
cards.definitions:
Instance and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with \(G=(V,E)\) connected. Write \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). Each \(e\in E\) has a weight \(w(e)\in\mathbb R\), with no integrality, magnitude, distinctness or sign promise. A spanning tree is a set \(T\subseteq E\) for which \((V,T)\) is connected and has no cycle; necessarily \(|T|=n-1\). Its weight is the finite real sum \(W(T)=\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\). A minimum spanning tree satisfies
\[\forall T'\subseteq E\text{ that is a spanning tree}:\quad W(T)\le W(T').\]
Connectedness ensures a spanning tree exists, and the finite collection of trees has a minimum. For \(n=1\), the graph has no edges and the required output is the empty tree. Equal or negative edge weights are allowed, and any minimizing tree is accepted. The algorithm need not output the numerical sum.

Explicit input and output. Input records give \(n,m\), the list of vertex labels, and an ordered list of \(m\) edge records. Edge \(j\), for \(1\le j\le m\), has endpoints \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and a handle for its opaque weight key. Pairs are not repeated, but their list order is arbitrary. The index \(j\) is the edge's distinct identifier. The input occupies \(\Theta(n+m)\) constant-size records. It is a full graph description rather than a circuit or oracle generating a larger graph. A weight key is supplied as an abstract atom, not a finite precision approximation or a binary expansion of its real value. The output lists exactly \(n-1\) distinct valid edge identifiers forming a minimum tree, in any order. No behavior is required on malformed or disconnected inputs.

Weight access. A weight handle can be stored, copied or retrieved in constant time. An instruction given two such handles returns their exact three-way real comparison: less, equal or greater. That instruction costs one operation independently of the real numbers. These are the only observations of weight values available to the algorithm. Weight handles identify their edge records; their numerical identifiers encode no information about the values. The program cannot inspect a weight's bits, add or subtract weights, multiply them, convert them to integers, hash their numerical representations, or compare arithmetic expressions involving weights. Copying a handle does not manufacture a new numerical key. The sum \(W(T)\) defines mathematical correctness, not an allowed machine instruction.

Nonweight machine operations. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\), and for input parameter \(N\) uses unsigned words of
\[\ell=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits for vertex labels, edge identifiers, counters and memory addresses. A word represents an integer from zero to \(2^\ell-1\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially zero; weight-key storage can equivalently keep the corresponding input handles. The input is read-only, and output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction touches a constant number of words or handles. Reading, writing, copying, comparing nonweight words and conditional branching cost one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^\ell\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, and bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT are also unit-cost. Logical shifts by fewer than \(\ell\) positions discard bits outside the word and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(\ell\) returns zero. Larger integer calculations require multiple words and their operations are charged. The program may use \(\ell\) as the machine word length. Word arithmetic is not arithmetic on the represented real weights.

Uniformity and time. There is no random input, random instruction, input-size advice, free preprocessing table or external computational oracle. The same finite program and word constant are used on every instance and edge-list order. All initialization it performs, comparisons, ordinary computation, generated tables and writing every output identifier count. Let \(T_A(G,w)\) be the number of these operations, with the edge-list representation understood as part of the input. The algorithm must halt with a correct tree on every valid instance. The time requirement is
\[\exists C>0\ \exists N_0\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall(G,w)\text{ with }n+m\ge N_0:\quad T_A(G,w)\le C(n+m).\]
The constants are independent of the graph, weights, density and representation order. This is deterministic worst-case sequential time. It is not an expectation over random graphs or over random choices, and an unbounded slowly growing extra factor does not count as linear.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic program and fixed word constant and prove termination, spanning-tree feasibility, exact minimum total weight and the displayed total-time bound for every connected simple graph and all real weight assignments. The proof must cover repeated and negative weights and the single-vertex case. If it uses decision trees or lookup tables, all work needed to produce and use them must be included.

A negative answer must rule out every correct deterministic program in the specified comparison-RAM model. Equivalently, for every word constant and every program that halts with a minimum tree on every valid input, prove that for each \(C>0\) and each \(N_0\) there is a valid instance and edge-list order with \(n+m\ge N_0\) on which the time exceeds \(C(n+m)\). A lower bound for one particular algorithm, one data structure, or a stricter pointer-only model does not establish this negation. A conditional lower bound must identify its unproved assumption and is not an unconditional resolution.

Expected-linear randomized algorithms, deterministic integer-weight algorithms that inspect weight bits, restricted graph classes and a linear number of comparisons with superlinear control overhead do not alone meet the target. Optimality relative to an unknown decision-tree complexity must include a linear bound on that complexity and the necessary implementation overhead to establish an affirmative answer. This card requires an exact minimum tree and an actual linear bound, with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.

cards.context:
A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is a basic optimization problem used in network design and clustering. The optimum can already be found in polynomial time; the unsettled issue is whether its exact deterministic computational cost can be only a constant multiple of the \(n\) vertex records and \(m\) edge records in the input.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for classical algorithms, but produces more information than the requested output. If the input graph is already a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of the weight order. For a triangle, omitting any largest-weight edge gives a minimum tree. The comparison lower bound for sorting all keys therefore does not automatically give a superlinear lower bound for this graph problem.

The optimum edge set can be identified using the order of the weights, even though its correctness is defined by a sum. The classical cut and cycle characterizations explain why numeric weight arithmetic is unnecessary. With ties there may be several minimum trees, all acceptable here. Distinct edge identifiers allow algorithms to impose a consistent order among equal keys, without imposing distinctness as an input promise.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle's deterministic comparison algorithm runs in \(O(m\alpha(m,n))\) time, apart from the trivial one-vertex case, where \(\alpha\) is an inverse-Ackermann function. It can be implemented on a pointer machine and assumes no numerical representation of the weights. Although its extra factor grows extremely slowly, the worst-case factor is unbounded asymptotically. If the input graph is already a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of the weight order. For a triangle, omitting any largest-weight edge gives a minimum tree. The optimum edge set can be identified using the order of the weights, even though its correctness is defined by a sum. The classical cut and cycle characterizations explain why numeric weight arithmetic is unnecessary. With ties there may be several minimum trees, all acceptable here. Distinct edge identifiers allow algorithms to impose a consistent order among equal keys, without imposing distinctness as an input promise.

source_formulation.text: The inherited card selects the classical uniform sequential comparison question: all connected simple graphs, arbitrary opaque real weights and deterministic worst-case O(n+m) total time. Karger–Klein–Tarjan explicitly distinguish this weight-access model from the integer representation model, and Pettie–Ramachandran distinguish optimal comparison complexity from a known linear time bound. cards.title: Černý conjecture
cards.formal: Does every synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with \(n\ge1\) states have a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\)? The statement quantifies over all finite nonempty alphabets. A reset word sends every possible initial state to the same state, under the transition model below.
cards.definitions: An automaton is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta)\), where \(|Q|=n\ge1\), \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty alphabet and \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\) is total. Extend it to words by \(\delta(q,\epsilon)=q\) and \(\delta(q,wa)=\delta(\delta(q,w),a)\). A word \(w\) is a reset word if \(|\{\delta(q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\); its length is its number of letters. Synchronizing means that at least one reset word exists. Its final state is not prescribed. Initial and accepting states play no role, and the empty word handles \(n=1\). There is no strong-connectivity, fixed-alphabet or other structural promise. Partial or nondeterministic automata, and synchronization of only a prescribed subset of states, are different models. No time bound for constructing the word is imposed. In the context, \(T(n)\) denotes the maximum shortest-reset-word length over all such synchronizing automata with \(n\) states; duplicate letter transformations can be removed, so this maximum exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that every synchronizing \(n\)-state automaton has a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\), or exhibit a synchronizing automaton and prove that every word up to that length fails to reset it.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

cards.context:
The selected binary question is the Černý conjecture. Its \((n-1)^2\) upper bound would match the classical worst-case family. A counterexample to the universal bound also answers this card; it need not determine the entire extremal function.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(L(D)=L(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma^{*}\), and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

cards.context:
All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq L\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(L=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.

The Geffert–Mereghetti–Pighizzini simulation gives \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states for unary two-way NFAs. It leaves a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial gap.
Kapoutsis characterizes polynomial-state simulation on short inputs by \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq L\)/poly, carefully distinguishing input-length restrictions and advice.

Guillon and coauthors give polynomial-size complementation using self-verifying 1-limited automata, with rewritable annotations; the unrestricted read-only determinization question remains open.

sentences: Two-way finite automata can reread their input by moving their head in either direction.
This project asks whether every n-state nondeterministic machine has an equivalent deterministic two-way machine with polynomially many states.
Both machines must agree on all finite words, with no restriction on input length.
Rereading sometimes replaces exponentially much one-way memory, but that observation does not supply a general simulation.

cards.title: Generalized star-height problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(L\subseteq \Sigma^{*}\) such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
cards.definitions: \(\Sigma^{*}\) is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from \(\varnothing , \varepsilon\), and the letters \(a\in \Sigma\) using binary union \(E\cup F\), concatenation EF, complement \(E^{c}\), and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, \(\{\varepsilon\}, \{a\}\), language union, all concatenations uv with \(u\in L(E)\) and \(v\in L(F), \Sigma^{*}\setminus L(E)\), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of \(L(E)\), including power zero \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(h(\varnothing )=h(\varepsilon )=h(a)=0, h(E\cup F)=h(\mathrm{EF})=\max \{h(E),h(F)\}, h(E^{c})=h(E)\), and \(h(E*)=h(E)+1\). Define \(h_{g}(L)=\min \{h(E):L(E)=L\}\), which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether \(h_{g}(L)>1\) for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation \((E^{c}\cup F^{c})^{c}\) and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
cards.why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.

cards.context:
Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over \(\Sigma =\{a,b\}\), the language of all words has the ordinary expression \((a\cup b)\)*, with a star. With complement, it is simply \(\varnothing ^{c}\) and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is \((\Sigma^{*}ab\Sigma^{*})^{c}\); replacing each displayed \(\Sigma^{*}\) by \(\varnothing ^{c}\) makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

Height zero does not capture all regular languages. Over the unary alphabet \(\{a\}\), the even-length language \((aa)\)* has generalized height exactly one. Its two-state automaton remembers length modulo two. Schützenberger’s theorem characterizes height zero through an aperiodic syntactic monoid, and this parity language has a nontrivial two-element group. Thus the first separation, between zero and one, is known; the question asks for the next separation.

The syntactic monoid packages how words behave inside arbitrary contexts: u and v are equivalent when puq belongs to L exactly when pvq does, for every pair of words p,q. Concatenation induces multiplication on the finitely many equivalence classes. A finite monoid is aperiodic when some exponent N makes \(x^{N}=x^{N+1}\) for every element x. Schützenberger’s characterization gives an effective algebraic test for star-freeness, but no corresponding complete height-one criterion is known.

The ordinary, or restricted, star-height problem disallows complement. In that setting, arbitrarily high heights exist and the minimum height is computable. These facts cannot be transferred to generalized height by reusing an ordinary expression or an automaton cycle measure: allowing complement introduces additional descriptions that the old lower-bound argument may not exclude. Pin’s problem page explicitly distinguishes these two versions and separately lists the existence of height two and the algorithmic computation of height.

Pin, Straubing and Thérien prove height at most one for several algebraic classes, including languages recognized by finite nilpotent groups of class at most two, and eliminate a proposed height-two example. They also show that every regular language is the inverse image of an ordinary height-one language under a suitable word morphism. That representation does not bound generalized height without an additional closure statement: inverse morphisms preserve regularity, but their preservation of generalized height one is part of the unresolved issue.

Bourne and Ruškuc extend the height-one territory using factor-counting arguments. Their results cover specified counting cases and languages recognized by Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. A factor here is a contiguous occurrence of a word, which differs from counting scattered subsequences. The theorem handles a substantial recognizing-semigroup class, while leaving the existence of a language above height one unresolved.

Daviaud and Paperman study languages generated from sets u* with a single word u, under Boolean or lattice operations and, in some cases, quotients. They give effective equational characterizations of those particular classes. These are deliberately restricted families inside the broader problem: a full height-one expression may take the star of an arbitrary star-free language and combine the resulting languages by concatenation and Boolean operations. Their paper describes its result as a step toward that larger structural challenge.

Cotumaccio’s 2025 account of connections between compressed indexing and automata again identifies generalized star height as an open structural question. It does not supply a new separation or universal flattening theorem. The relevance extends beyond a formal-expression puzzle: a solution would clarify how finite-state iteration, modular behaviour and Boolean operations interact, while allowing descriptions to grow arbitrarily large.

cards.title: Decidability of equivalence for unambiguous context-free grammars
cards.formal: Is it decidable, given two finite context-free grammars \(G_1,G_2\) over the same finite terminal alphabet and promised that both are unambiguous, whether \(L(G_1)=L(G_2)\)?
cards.definitions: A context-free grammar \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\) has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of productions \(A\to u\), with \(A\in V\) and \(u\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed. A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \(S\) whose nonterminal nodes expand by productions; its terminal leaves read from left to right form the generated word, possibly empty. The language \(L(G)\subseteq\Sigma^*\) consists of words with such a tree. Unambiguous means at most one parse tree for each word, not at most one order of expanding a fixed tree. Both grammars, alphabet lists and full production strings are explicit finite inputs with binary symbol identifiers and delimiters; duplicate written productions are identified. The decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that terminates on every syntactically valid pair and is correct whenever both grammars satisfy the promise. On pairs violating the promise it may return either answer. Invalid syntax may be rejected. It receives no proof of unambiguity and need not decide that promise. There is no running-time bound, determinism promise for the grammars or restriction to regular or unary languages.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such a decision machine exists, or a Lean proof that the promised equivalence problem is undecidable. A result for deterministic pushdown presentations, comparison with only a finite automaton, or a semidecision procedure for inequivalence does not settle the complete two-grammar question.
cards.why: This basic equivalence problem tests the algorithmic power of unique parsing beyond deterministic context-free language descriptions.

cards.title: Word problem for one-relation monoids
cards.formal: Is the uniform word problem for ordinary one-relation monoids decidable? Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, given any finite alphabet \(A\) and four finite words \(u,v,s,t\in A^*\), always halts and decides whether \(s\) and \(t\) represent the same element of the monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\)? The presentation and the word pair are all parts of the input; no running-time bound is prescribed.
cards.definitions:
The free monoid \(A^*\) consists of all finite literal strings over \(A\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as multiplication and \(\varepsilon\) as identity. The monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\) is the quotient \(A^*/{\equiv}\), where \(\equiv\) is the least equivalence relation containing \(u\equiv v\) and satisfying \(p\equiv q\Rightarrow xpy\equiv xqy\) for all words \(x,y\). Equivalently, \(s\equiv t\) if and only if some finite sequence \(s=w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_k=t\) exists in which every adjacent pair is \((xuy,xvy)\) or \((xvy,xuy)\) for some \(x,y\in A^*\). A zero-step sequence is allowed.

The four words are fully supplied literal strings, not variables to be instantiated by unknown strings. The two relation sides and the tested words may be empty. Replacing an empty side means inserting the other side at a gap in the current finite word. The relation may have equal sides and may preserve or change length. The alphabet itself may be empty, in which case every word is empty. There are no inverse symbols with automatic cancellation, group axioms, cancellation laws or commutativity laws beyond consequences of the single stated monoid relation.

The input explicitly gives an integer alphabet size \(a\ge0\), identifies \(A\) with \(\{1,\ldots,a\}\), and lists all four words with binary letter indices and lengths. This is finite ordinary string input, with malformed encodings rejectable. One ordinary deterministic program must give exact YES/NO answers for all valid presentations and all pairs, terminating on both answers. It receives no oracle, nonuniform advice, random coins or unbounded precomputed data for a presentation. No numerical approximation arises. This is uniform decidability across presentations; a separate non-effectively chosen algorithm for each fixed presentation has different quantifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that the displayed language of presentation-and-word-pair instances is decidable by a total computable function, or a proof of its undecidability. A positive proof must formalize finite words, the single-relation contextual congruence, finite encoding and a uniform algorithm whose termination and both correctness directions hold for all allowed empty and nonempty inputs. A negative reduction must stay inside ordinary one-relation monoids and preserve equality in both directions. A single fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem suffices for a negative answer but is stronger than necessary to refute uniform decidability. A semidecision procedure that halts only on equal words, an unproved termination claim, an exponential derivation-length lower bound, or a negative theorem for inverse monoids, submonoid membership or equations with unknowns does not by itself settle the target. No Lean resolution is asserted by this review.
cards.why: A foundational decidability boundary for rewriting: can reachability under one literal reversible string rule already escape every terminating uniform algorithm?

cards.context:
This is a minimal string-transformation problem. There is only one reversible replacement rule, and it can be applied inside any surrounding context. Starting with a word, repeated replacements can generate many others. Equality asks whether the target lies in this reachability set. The alphabet symbols themselves have no hidden arithmetic meaning; any complicated computation would have to emerge from overlaps and repeated applications of this one rule.

An equality has a finite certificate: a sequence of contextual applications of the defining relation connecting the two words. Inequality has no analogous certificate supplied by the presentation itself. A long search with no successful derivation does not decide whether one exists, since intermediate words can have unbounded length.

Length-preserving relations, where \(|u|=|v|\), form a decidable special case. The general problem allows length-changing replacements. Termination of an oriented shortening rule is not sufficient by itself: different irreducible words may still represent the same element. The requested algorithm has no efficiency requirement, so a large computable time bound would still be a positive answer.

The surrounding algebra offers major positive results. Magnus proved decidability for one-relator groups in 1932. For ordinary monoids, classical work handles important cases such as a single relation equating a word to the identity, and presentations satisfying appropriate cycle-free conditions. Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family \(\langle a,b | baa(ba)^{N}=a\rangle\) for \(N\ge 2\) with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

Foniqi–Gray–Nyberg-Brodda prove undecidability of submonoid membership for families of one-relation monoids, in a paper published online in 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume. Submonoid membership asks whether an element equals some product of members of a supplied finite generating list. That existential product choice is absent when comparing just two supplied words.

The August 2026 Diophantine result proves undecidability of solving systems of equations with unknown monoid elements and fixed coefficients in certain one-relation monoids. The word problem is a special case of that broader task, so the broader negative theorem does not imply undecidability of the special case on this card. This also distinguishes equality modulo one literal relation from ordinary word equations over a free monoid.

The current card retains its saved uniform target: the presentation varies with the input to one machine. The sources often phrase the general question as decidability for every fixed one-relation monoid. An affirmative uniform theorem would imply all those individual conclusions; a uniform negative theorem need not exhibit a single fixed undecidable monoid. The August 2026 inverse-monoid paper explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open, and the bounded subsequent search found no matching uniform resolution.

progress.text: Magnus solves the one-relator group word problem; later work solves major ordinary-monoid special cases, without providing a general procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda surveys the unresolved problem, reduction methods, special cases and gaps in earlier claimed arguments.
The survey’s corrigendum fixes historical attributions and technical wording, including nontermination versus literal looping of Adian’s procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda gives monadic one-relation monoids with exponential Dehn functions but decidable word problems, separating short derivations from decidability.
Gray–Reilly prove undecidability for certain two-generator one-relator inverse monoids; their introduction explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open.
The published membership results concern existential membership in generated submonoids, rather than equality of two specified words.
The Diophantine preprint proves undecidability of equation solvability with unknown elements in some one-relation monoids, a broader predicate than this card.
The audit preserves the uniform ordinary-monoid target and score 96, fixes complete word notation and encodings, and adds full Lean acceptance and later-result scope checks.

sentences: An ordinary one-relation monoid identifies words using one fixed reversible literal replacement rule in arbitrary surrounding contexts.
The question asks whether a single algorithm can decide equality of any two words when the alphabet and defining relation are also supplied.
Empty words and length-changing relations are allowed, and the algorithm must halt on unequal pairs as well as equal ones.

cards.title: A logic capturing polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a logic L with decidable syntax and isomorphism-invariant semantics on finite relational structures such that its sentences define exactly the polynomial-time decidable Boolean properties, and an effective compiler maps each sentence to a correct polynomial-time evaluation algorithm with a polynomial running-time bound?
cards.definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.
cards.why: The central descriptive-complexity question of characterizing feasible computation without supplying an arbitrary order.

cards.context:
A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. Thus a proof that no such logic exists would also separate P from NP.

cards.title: Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every input consisting of an integer \(k\ge1\), integer coefficients \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), and integer initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(u_t=0\) for some integer \(t\ge0\), where the infinite sequence is uniquely defined by \[u_{t+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j u_{t+j}\qquad(t=0,1,2,\ldots)?\] The order \(k\) is part of the input and is unrestricted; no time or space bound is requested.
cards.definitions: Use input alphabet \(\{0,1,+,-,\#\}\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\) be its ordinary base-two expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Encode an integer \(z\) by a plus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) if \(z\ge0\), and by a minus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(-z)\) if \(z<0\); negative zero is invalid. A valid input is \(\operatorname{bin}(k)\), then exactly \(k\) signed coefficient fields in order, then exactly \(k\) signed initial-value fields in order, separated by one \(\#\) between consecutive fields, with no other symbols or trailing separator. The first field has \(k\ge1\). Output 1 means that a zero occurs at some nonnegative index, including among the initial values; output 0 means that every term at a nonnegative index is nonzero. The machine must halt with one of these two outputs on every valid input and reject every malformed input with output 0. This decidable syntax convention does not affect the underlying decidability question. A deterministic Turing machine has one finite transition table, a finite alphabet and finitely many work tapes; it has no randomness, external oracle, advice or input-dependent program. The sequence values are exact integers with no bound on their magnitude, and the same fixed coefficients apply at every index. The listed recurrence need not have the smallest possible order. Coefficients and initial values may vanish, all may be zero, and \(c_0=0\) is allowed; forward evolution is still uniquely defined. In particular, neither distinct characteristic roots nor a non-degeneracy assumption is promised. No upper bound on the index of a possible zero is supplied. This is a discrete-time existence-of-a-zero question, with indices \(0,1,2,\ldots\); negative or real-valued indices and nonnegativity of all terms are different targets.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a total decision machine exists, with termination and correctness for every valid input and rejection of malformed strings, or a Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Equivalently, the language of valid encodings whose sequences contain a zero must be proved decidable or undecidable. A negative answer must rule out every total deterministic decider, not merely give an input on which one proposed program fails. A positive answer has to decide both the zero and zero-free cases uniformly over all orders; a semidecision procedure, a bounded-index algorithm, a theorem for a fixed order, or conditional termination under an unproved number-theoretic assumption does not settle the full target. A complexity lower bound such as NP-hardness does not prove undecidability. No polynomial bound, bound on the first zero, or enumeration of the entire zero set is required as the output.
cards.why: Skolem asks whether exact reachability of zero is decidable for the simplest class of discrete linear recurrences with finite integer descriptions. The question connects arithmetic with verification of linear loops, matrix dynamics, automata and stochastic systems, and serves as a common unresolved decision problem to which other verification tasks are compared.
