references.locator: Version 1, 22 January; primary author/arXiv abstracts and history read for scope only. The author page lists FOCS 2026; no publication date or full-proof verification is inferred. The stated result is query-based property testing, not a PAC learner

cards.context:
A DNF accepts a point when at least one conjunction of feature conditions holds. Learning predicts these labels from observations without receiving the rules. The unknown distribution can concentrate its probability on any subset of the Boolean cube, so uniform-input arguments do not automatically extend to this task.

The obstacle is computational rather than a shortage of samples: the finite DNF class admits sample complexity \(O((ns+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\). This statistical guarantee does not give a polynomial-time learner. The 2025 survey explicitly separates sample complexity from the cost of producing an evaluable hypothesis.

For each fixed term bound \(s\), a runtime \(n^{O(s)}\) is polynomial in \(n\), but the required single polynomial in both \(n\) and \(s\) is stronger. Servedio’s Theorem 8 records the general upper bound \(2^{\widetilde O(n^{1/3}\log s)}\), with accuracy and confidence dependence suppressed as specified in that survey; the tilde hides polylogarithmic factors. This remains superpolynomial for polynomially many terms.

Improper learning allows hypotheses outside the DNF class. A lower bound for outputting a small DNF can therefore leave this question open. Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz give an improper-learning hardness result under their random-K-SAT refutation assumption, including polynomially growing term bounds. That assumption is not an established unconditional lower bound.

Daniely–Vardi’s Theorem 3 rules out efficient learning of DNFs with a superconstant number of terms under their Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators. Their learning definition permits efficiently evaluable hypotheses outside the target class. The local-generator hypothesis is a specific average-case assumption, not merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or an unconditional theorem.

The 2025 faster exact learner of Alman and coauthors has access to membership and equivalence queries. A membership query obtains the target value at a chosen point; an equivalence query can provide a counterexample to a proposed hypothesis. Those access guarantees differ from an independent random-example stream, even when the question still concerns small DNFs.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering result obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning in the PQ distribution-shift framework under a uniform training distribution. Its predictor may use a selector to abstain, and training labels and unlabeled test data have distinct roles. Those distribution, runtime and output guarantees do not supply the polynomial-time distribution-free predictor required here.

The January 2026 relative-error DNF result is a property tester: it distinguishes membership in the class from the specified notion of distance using function-query access. Testing whether an unknown function is a DNF is a different output task from learning an accurate predictive circuit from random examples.

Every \(k\)-junta, a Boolean function depending on at most \(k\) coordinates, has a DNF representation with at most \(2^k\) terms. Consequently, a learner meeting this target would give a learner polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\) for juntas, including under the uniform distribution. This implication does not assert that learning juntas alone suffices for general DNF learning.

source_formulation.text: The inherited question comes from the first paragraph of Feldman’s 2012 introduction: polynomial-time PAC learning of polynomial-size DNFs from random examples under an arbitrary unknown distribution. The retained size-sensitive statement permits improper learning. The integer learning parameters, explicit circuit syntax and charged example-access convention specify that target rather than adding query access or restricting the hypothesis to DNF.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected 2025 survey retains the distribution-free computational gap. The 2016 and 2021 improper-learning lower bounds retain random-SAT or local-PRG assumptions. Current 2025/2026 exact-query, property-testing and PQ-learning results have different access, output, distribution or runtime guarantees. No verified unconditional solution of the retained target was found in bounded primary-source checks; recent proofs were not independently certified.

cards.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that every Boolean \(k\)-junta on \(n\) variables can be learned from independent uniform noiseless examples in time polynomial in \(n,2^k\) and inverse error? Explicitly, for all integers \(n\ge1\), \(0\le k\le n\), \(t\ge3\), and every \(k\)-junta \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), the learner receives \(1^n,1^k,1^t\) and an independent-example oracle \(\operatorname{EX}_f\). Every execution takes at most \(B(n+2^k+t)^C\) steps and outputs an ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) for which \[\Pr_{A,\,\operatorname{EX}_f}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23.\] The exponent \(C\), constant \(B\) and machine are independent of \(n,k,t,f\). This preserves the existing full \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) target; it is not merely a separate polynomial-time statement for every fixed \(k\).
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A \(k\)-junta is a Boolean function for which there exist an unknown subset \(S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}\subseteq[n]\), \(r\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean table \(g:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_r})\quad\text{for all }x\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Neither \(S\) nor \(g\) is given to the learner. No monotonicity, sparsity of the truth table or lower bound on variable influence is assumed. For \(k=0\), the class consists of the two constant functions, using the unique empty input to \(g\). The public \(k\) is only an upper bound on the number of relevant coordinates; it need not be the minimal support size.

\(U_n\) gives each binary vector probability \(2^{-n}\). Each call to \(\operatorname{EX}_f\) supplies a new pair \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim U_n\), independent of all previous draws and the learner’s fair random coins. The unknown target is fixed before the data are drawn. The learner can request further independent examples adaptively, but cannot choose their inputs, obtain membership-query labels, or request coupled or neighboring examples. Labels are exact noiseless bits. The outer probability measures confidence over the complete learning execution; the inner probability is zero-one prediction error on a fresh independent input. Reciprocals of positive integers suffice to represent arbitrary desired positive error tolerances up to polynomial rounding overhead. The fixed confidence is \(2/3\).

The output is a finite acyclic ordinary Boolean circuit on the \(n\) input bits, using two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants with a fixed effective binary encoding. It may depend on all coordinates and need not itself be a \(k\)-junta; this is improper learning. It is evaluated without the training oracle and with no stored target-dependent state other than its output description. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, receiving the displayed public integers in unary. All example reading, computation, stored-data access, fair random bits and output writing count in the worst-case bit-time bound, which also bounds the number of example requests and output length. The example generator’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Circuit evaluation is polynomial in the written circuit size under this encoding. Repeated access to stored examples and any polynomial amount of memory within the time bound are allowed. The requirement is predictive approximation; it does not require identifying the exact relevant set, giving a minimum representation or recovering every truth-table entry.

Polynomial dependence on \(2^k\) permits an exponential dependence on the number of relevant variables, since an arbitrary \(k\)-bit table already has \(2^k\) entries. It excludes a degree of \(n\) that grows with \(k\). For every fixed \(c>0\), the displayed guarantee would in particular be polynomial in \(n,t\) for all \(k\le c\log_2 n\); an algorithm that only handles each constant \(k\) with its own exponent need not satisfy it. The accuracy target is the explicitly bounded rational error \(1/t\); the problem asks for exact existence of the learner and universal exponent rather than a numerical optimal value.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof that such \(A,B,C\) exist, or prove the complete negation: for every proposed uniform machine and universal constants, some allowed \(n,k,t,f\) violates the worst-case resource bound, finite hypothesis condition or the stated PAC probability. A positive answer must handle all Boolean junta tables and all support sizes up to \(n\) with one exponent independent of \(k\). A learner using membership queries, correlated random-walk examples, a randomly perturbed marginal distribution, or only monotone targets does not meet the specified interface. A statistical-query, limited-memory or specified-neural-training lower bound does not exclude every allowed machine. Conditional cryptographic hardness must retain its unproved premise and is not the unconditional negation. Neither exact support recovery nor a prescribed proper output is an additional obligation.
cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

cards.context:
A junta uses only a few of the available input features, but its dependence on those features can be completely arbitrary. The problem asks for an efficient predictor from passive observations. It separates the small information content of the hidden rule from the computational cost of locating useful features among many irrelevant ones.

The finite class contains at most \((k+1)n^k2^{2^k}\) functions. At constant confidence, realizable finite-class learning therefore needs only \(O((2^k+k\log(n+1)+\log(k+1)+1)/\varepsilon)\) examples information-theoretically. This fits the desired polynomial resource scale; the unresolved requirement is efficient computation with those examples.

Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio give exact learning in \(n^{(\omega/(\omega+1))k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,\log(1/\delta))\) time, where \(\omega\) is a valid matrix-multiplication exponent. Using the exponent available in their paper gives roughly \(n^{0.704k}\) times polynomial factors. Their model uses independent uniform examples, so this is progress in the required access model.

Valiant’s Corollary 7 improves noiseless junta learning to a bound below \(n^{0.60k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k)\) for the matrix-multiplication exponent and constants used there. Servedio’s November 2025 survey still reports the roughly \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark. The exponent of the ambient dimension continues to grow with support size, so this is not the universal polynomial in the formal statement.

Individual-coordinate correlation can vanish even for a relevant coordinate, as in the parity of three selected bits. That illustrates a limitation of certain correlation statistics, not an unconditional lower bound against all example-based learners: noiseless parity itself has an efficient algebraic learner. Statistical-query restrictions must remain distinct from unrestricted observation of the actual samples.

Membership-query algorithms and monotone-junta learners have stronger positive guarantees under their respective conditions. Membership queries let the learner choose which inputs are labeled, while monotonicity restricts the possible truth tables. Neither condition is assumed here.

Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper concerns distributions whose probability mass function depends on a small coordinate set and relates that density-learning task to sparse noisy parity. Its introduction separately describes the persistent difficulty of noiseless Boolean function learning under uniform examples. The distribution-learning equivalence is not a resolution of this card’s prediction problem.

The inherited OpenReview pointer has now been identified as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields, NeurIPS 2025. Its introduction explicitly retains the difficult uniform-example question. Its positive Theorem 1.3 assumes a smoothed Markov random field, a known bounded-degree dependency graph and the stated bounded-width parameters, with success probability also taken over the random external-field perturbation. Even though the unperturbed uniform distribution is a Markov random field, a guarantee over positive random smoothing does not imply a guarantee at that exact unperturbed distribution.

Cornacchia–Mikulincer–Mossel’s May 2026 Theorem 2 studies labeled samples along a lazy random walk on the hypercube. It gives nearly linear ambient-dimension sample dependence for each fixed support size, with the stated target-dependent constants. Consecutive examples are correlated even if each has a uniform marginal. An independent-example source does not provide that temporal information, so the theorem concerns a different learning interface.

A \(k\)-junta has a decision-tree or DNF representation of size at most \(2^k\) under the usual leaf/term convention, with polynomial overhead if literal occurrences are counted. Efficient uniform-example learning for those larger representation classes would therefore imply the requested bound. This explains the junta problem’s role as a basic obstacle within computational learning theory.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, inherited through the consolidation of TCS-0023, asks for polynomial-time uniform learning beyond constant support size, or hardness under a natural complexity assumption. The retained card asks for the specific stronger bound \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) for every \(k\). A positive answer handles \(k=O(\log n)\); success only in a slower-growing regime or a conditional negative answer is not the same assertion. This historical source remains a related milestone, and the earlier consolidation and reserved identifier are preserved as provenance.

cards.title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that, for every \(n,s\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by a decision tree with at most \(s\) nodes, \(A\), given \(1^n,1^s,1^t\) and independent uniform examples labeled by \(f\), runs on every execution for at most \(B(n+s+t)^C\) steps and outputs a Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{A,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23?\] The hypothesis may be an arbitrary efficiently evaluable circuit. The target remains the previously selected polynomial-time sample-only uniform-PAC question; reciprocal-integer error \(\varepsilon=1/t\) makes the accuracy encoding explicit.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by a coordinate index in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and has two children, with outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), evaluation follows the edge specified by the queried bit at each internal node until it reaches a leaf, whose bit is the output. Coordinates may occur repeatedly and there is no depth, monotonicity, balance, or randomness promise on the hidden tree. Size counts all nodes, as in the existing card. A full branching binary tree with \(\ell\) leaves has \(2\ell-1\) nodes, so the leaf-count convention used by the backdoor-defense source changes this polynomial-size question only by a constant factor. The size bound and input dimension are public; the target tree, its structure and its node labels are not supplied.

\(U_n\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Each example request yields a fresh independent \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim U_n\), under one fixed target. Labels are exact and noiseless. Requests may be scheduled adaptively, but the learner cannot choose the input to be labeled or require correlations between successive inputs. In particular, there is no membership oracle, equivalence oracle or free access to the tree representation. The learner uses independent fair random bits and no length-dependent advice. Its guarantee is required for every target tree, rather than for a random tree or a randomly perturbed input distribution. The outer probability is confidence over the training draws and internal coins; the inner error probability concerns a fresh independent uniform input.

An output hypothesis is a finite acyclic circuit on the same \(n\) bits, using two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates in a fixed effective binary encoding. It need not be a tree or have size at most \(s\). The output is evaluated without further samples, the hidden target or any unreported target-dependent state. This is improper predictive learning, not exact tree identification or minimum-size reconstruction. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with unary public parameters; every bit operation, request, example read, stored-data access, random bit and output bit is counted. One fixed worst-case bound applies across all parameters and sample histories; the same bound also limits sample count and output length. Circuit evaluation takes polynomial time in the written circuit size. The example source’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Unlimited computation on polynomially many examples does not meet the requirement.

The error parameter ranges over \(1/t\), \(t\ge3\). For any desired real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choosing \(t=\max\{3,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\) yields error at most \(\varepsilon\) with only polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Thus this encoding retains the ordinary arbitrary-accuracy learning target without treating an arbitrarily long rational spelling as a constant-cost input. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The universal polynomial has no degree depending on \(s\), tree depth, the particular target or the accuracy parameter. The problem is a yes/no existence statement; there is no unspecified numerical optimization precision.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the stated uniform learner and universal polynomial bound exist, or prove their logical negation: every proposed machine and constants fail for some allowed dimension, size, accuracy and target, in either the worst-case resource guarantee or the PAC success condition. A positive answer must use only independent uniform labeled examples and cover every target tree. Proper-learning hardness, minimum-consistent-tree hardness, or a lower bound for one greedy heuristic does not rule out the allowed arbitrary circuit output. A result under an unproved computational assumption proves only the corresponding conditional negation. Membership-query learning, random-tree learning, smoothed-distribution learning and correlated-example algorithms have different access or target promises and are not accepted as a resolution of the displayed statement.
cards.why: Settle the sample-only computational learnability of a canonical interpretable Boolean model.

cards.context:
Decision trees describe classification through simple successive tests of individual input bits. A small tree may nevertheless hide complicated interactions among the variables. The question asks whether uniform random observations suffice for efficient prediction, even when the learner is free to return a representation different from a tree.

At a fixed node bound, the number of tree descriptions is at most exponential in a polynomial in the size and logarithm of the input dimension. Consequently the realizable information-theoretic sample requirement is polynomial in size, dimension and inverse error. The desired theorem concerns computation as well as data, rather than mere statistical identifiability.

A tree with at most \(s\) nodes has at most \(s\) leaves and can be expressed as a DNF with at most \(s\) terms. Known uniform-example DNF learners therefore provide quasipolynomial algorithms in the polynomial-size regime, as summarized by Servedio’s Theorem 13. That is a useful general upper bound, but a dimension exponent growing logarithmically with size or inverse error is not the requested one fixed polynomial.

Kalai–Teng’s Theorem 1 learns every target tree efficiently for most product distributions obtained by randomly perturbing their coordinate means by a fixed positive amount. Its probability is over both the perturbation and the training examples. The exact vector of uniform means is a particular unperturbed point, so success for almost all perturbed means does not imply the guarantee at that point. The theorem is explicitly improper and outputs a polynomial threshold function.

The ITCS 2025 source again states that efficient uniform-PAC learning of polynomial-size trees is unknown in the sample-only model. Its positive backdoor-defense theorem gives the defender the represented tree, which allows direct examination and evaluation. That observation model differs from receiving only labeled examples of a hidden tree. A fast detector with the representation supplied is not a PAC learner for this card.

Membership queries make uniform decision-tree learning easier because they provide labels at chosen inputs. Proper-learning problems impose a different restriction by requiring a tree output. This target has the passive observation interface and permits arbitrary Boolean circuit output; hardness for a restricted output class cannot be transferred just by matching the words “decision tree learning.”

The checked May 2026 paper on product spaces explicitly allows label queries at arbitrary inputs in §3. Its main size bound also depends on the optimal tree’s maximum and average depths and can be quasipolynomial even for logarithmic-depth trees. These are useful guarantees for the studied greedy procedure, but neither the interface nor the bound supplies the full polynomial sample-only learner.

Every \(k\)-junta has a decision tree with at most \(2^{k+1}-1\) nodes. Thus the desired learner would give time polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon\) for arbitrary juntas from uniform examples. The 2025 survey describes that junta problem as a continuing obstacle. This is a consequence of the tree-learning target, not an added promise that the tree must depend on few variables.

cards.title: Existence of one-way functions
cards.formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to \{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer \(d\ge 1\), there is \(n_{0}\) with \(\Pr [f(I(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)]\le n^{- d}\) for all \(n\ge n_{0}\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
cards.definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(n\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.
cards.why: Asks for the unconditional existence of the basic computational asymmetry underlying much of modern cryptography.

cards.context:
Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

Suppose f keeps the first \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

An inverter that succeeds with probability \(1/n^{10}\) still violates the requirement. A probability such as \(2^{- n}\) is negligible, while \(1/n^{10}\) is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

One-way functions would imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), since \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would permit efficient search for a polynomial-length preimage. Whether \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone implies their existence is separately recorded in TCS-0022. One-way functions are equivalent to several basic cryptographic primitives, including pseudorandom generators and suitable private-key encryption, but it is not known whether they suffice for public-key encryption; that implication is TCS-6545. The present question assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) nor any candidate’s hardness.

Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(\lambda\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.
cards.why: This asks whether the minimal generic assumption supporting private-key cryptography also supports encryption to a receiver whose encryption key is public. It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.

cards.context:
Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

The target retains the saved one-bit message convention. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The card permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the related key-agreement card has a separate conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this card.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The card therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) imply the existence of a classical one-way function secure against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inversion? Precisely, under that premise alone, must there exist one total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*}\]
such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every real constant \(c>0\), there is an integer \(N\ge1\) for which every \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,r}\!\left[z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad z=I(1^n,f(x);r)\right]\le n^{-c}?\]
Here \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on length-\(n\) binary strings, and \(r\) denotes the inverter’s independent fair random coins. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as successful inversion. The function must be fixed before the inverter and security exponent are chosen.
cards.definitions:
All computation is by ordinary multitape Turing machines with fixed finite programs and finite tape alphabets, unit-cost transitions and explicitly encoded inputs/outputs. There are no oracles, nonuniform advice strings, quantum operations or external uncounted computations. Polynomial time means a bound \(a(m+1)^d\) on every input of length \(m\), for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on the machine. Reading input, evaluating functions, generating random bits and writing outputs are included in the running time.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) lies in \(\mathrm{P}\) if one deterministic polynomial-time machine decides membership on every input. It lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is equivalent to existence of a binary certificate of polynomially bounded length accepted by one deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The verifier is total on all input/certificate pairs. The premise compares these uniform total decision classes, not circuit classes or average-case classes.

The function \(f\) is computed by one deterministic machine in polynomial time on every binary string, including the empty string; its output length is consequently polynomially bounded. No length-preserving or injectivity requirement is imposed. Its description is public and may be built into an inverter’s fixed program. Security is required at positive input lengths \(n\).

An inverter \(I\) receives the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,y)\), with the input length \(n\) in unary and \(y\) a binary string. It has one fixed program, obtains independent unbiased coin bits, and halts within one polynomial in \(n+|y|+1\) on every input and every coin sequence. It outputs a finite binary string or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Its polynomial may depend on \(I\) but not on \(n,y\). An output of the wrong length, \(\bot\), or a string whose image differs from \(y\) is a failure. The retained convention is same-length inversion: a preimage must have the sampled input length \(n\). The original sampled \(x\) need not be recovered if another such preimage exists.

The experiment first draws \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) inputs, evaluates \(y=f(x)\), and runs \(I\) with fresh independent random coins. Thus outputs with more length-\(n\) preimages are encountered more frequently; \(y\) is not sampled uniformly from the range. The probability is a finite exact average, since the inverter has an all-path polynomial clock. The constants in the forward evaluation bound and the inverter bound can differ.

Negligible inversion probability means exactly the quantifier order
\[\exists f\ \forall I\ \forall c>0\ \exists N=N(f,I,c)\ \forall n\ge N.\]
Neither the inverter nor \(f\) can vary with the input length, although each may use the supplied length in its computation. Security at only infinitely many lengths is not the target. Failure of one-wayness for a fixed \(f\) means that some single polynomial-time inverter has success greater than \(n^{-c}\), for some fixed \(c>0\), at arbitrarily large lengths; the logical negation does not demand success at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication in the statement or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, a total function with one uniform polynomial-time evaluator and the stated eventual negligible-success guarantee against every permitted inverter. No additional circuit lower bound, average-case hardness assumption or conjectured cryptographic primitive may be left unproved. The proof may use the premise without proving it separately.

A negative proof must establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) and show that for every total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\), there exist a single permitted inverter \(I\) and a constant \(c>0\) such that for every threshold \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has inversion success greater than \(n^{-c}\). An oracle separation, a barrier to one reduction technique, or an efficient inverter for a particular candidate is insufficient. The target is an existence implication and imposes no black-box-construction requirement or prescribed proof method.
cards.why: One-way functions are a basic foundation for computational pseudorandomness and cryptography. This question asks whether a worst-case separation between decision and verification already forces a function whose efficiently generated outputs resist inversion on average, without a separate cryptographic assumption.

cards.context:
Existence of one-way functions implies \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The converse asks for much more than a function with occasional difficult inputs: the security experiment generates inputs uniformly, and every efficient inverter must have negligible overall success at all sufficiently large lengths. Worst-case inversion difficulty by itself does not give that distributional guarantee.

Average-case decision hardness and one-wayness have distinct requirements. The former can concern a language paired with a chosen feasible instance distribution. Here instances are images of uniform inputs under the same efficiently computable function whose inversion is tested. The adversary may exploit collisions and only needs to find any permitted preimage; hard reconstruction of the original sampled input is not enough.

Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby establish that one-way functions suffice for cryptographic pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. A cryptographic generator efficiently expands uniform random bits so that polynomial-time statistical tests cannot distinguish its outputs from uniform strings with nonnegligible advantage. This explains the broad consequences of the primitive without adding encryption, a trapdoor or injectivity to this question.

Known nonadaptive oracle-reduction barriers show that certain reductions from NP-complete worst-case problems to average inversion would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such reductions choose all their oracle questions before receiving answers and must work for every oracle satisfying the average-success promise. The barrier concerns that reduction class; it does not establish the negation of the unrestricted implication.

Liu–Pass give an unconditional equivalence between one-way functions and a particular boundary-hardness condition for randomized time-bounded description complexity. Their corresponding statement for deterministic description complexity uses an exponential circuit-hardness assumption. An equivalence with a specialized hardness condition does not by itself establish that condition from \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\); the inspected paper explicitly retains this missing connection.

The April 2026 Liu–Mazor–Pass paper derives conditional pseudorandom generators and restricted zero-knowledge consequences from hardness of specific gap-description problems. A conditional generator’s seed distribution may be inefficient to sample, whereas an ordinary cryptographic generator uses uniform seeds. The paper retains additional hardness hypotheses and says that obtaining ordinary one-way functions from plain worst-case gap hardness remains beyond its results.

The eventual security requirement matters to both sides of the question. To disprove one-wayness of a candidate, a fixed inverter with noticeable success at arbitrarily large lengths is enough. To prove one-wayness, security on a sparse infinite subsequence is insufficient. The requested implication therefore cannot be replaced by an infinitely-often variant without changing the target.

cards.title: Exponential share-size lower bounds for perfect secret sharing
cards.formal:
An access structure specifies which groups of participants may recover a secret; a perfect scheme gives exact recovery to those groups and no information to all other groups. Precise definitions appear in Model & notation. Is the following proposition true?
\[
\exists c>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \exists\Gamma_n\subseteq 2^{[n]}:
\quad\forall\text{ perfect schemes for }\Gamma_n,\qquad
\max_{i\in[n]}\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\ge 2^{cn}.
\]
Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the secret is one uniform bit, \(\Gamma_n\) is a monotone access structure with \(\varnothing\notin\Gamma_n\) and \([n]\in\Gamma_n\), and \(\mathcal S_i\) is participant \(i\)'s finite share alphabet. Here \(n_0\) is an integer, and the constants are universal. Sharing and reconstruction may be nonlinear and computationally unbounded.
cards.definitions:
A monotone access structure \(\Gamma\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is a collection of authorized subsets such that \(A\in\Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq[n]\) imply \(B\in\Gamma\).

A perfect scheme is a joint probability distribution of a uniform secret \(B\in\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_i\in\mathcal S_i\), where every \(\mathcal S_i\) is finite and nonempty. For each authorized \(A\), a deterministic map from \(\prod_{i\in A}\mathcal S_i\) to \(\{0,1\}\) recovers \(B\) with probability one. For every unauthorized \(A\), the distributions of \((X_i)_{i\in A}\) conditioned on \(B=0\) and on \(B=1\) are identical. Arbitrary joint distributions are allowed; there is no field or linearity restriction.

The cost of a share is \(\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\) bits, and the scheme's cost is the largest of these costs. This measures alphabet size, not Shannon entropy. Rounding to an integer encoding length does not change the exponential-existence question. The access structures need not be efficiently recognizable, and the schemes need not be uniformly constructible. The statement concerns all sufficiently large integer participant counts, with one positive constant \(c\) chosen first.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified exponential lower bound, or a complete proof of its logical negation. A lower bound restricted to linear schemes or to bounded-complexity reconstruction does not meet the universal scheme quantifier. A merely superpolynomial lower bound does not establish the stated exponential bound.
cards.why: This asks whether some access-control policies inherently require exponentially large pieces of a one-bit secret, even with unlimited computation. It would distinguish an intrinsic information cost from limitations of the constructions currently available.

cards.context:
For a threshold policy, any sufficiently large group can recover a secret and smaller groups learn nothing. General policies can specify much less regular combinations of participants. The conjecture asks whether that freedom forces an exponential storage cost in the worst case.

Larsen and Simkin study the exponential lower-bound conjecture attributed to Beimel. Their theorem forces either large shares or a large description of reconstruction; it does not remove the reconstruction restriction needed for an unconditional share-size lower bound.

Recent linear and multilinear lower bounds concern schemes whose algebraic structure restricts the sharing or reconstruction maps. Such restrictions are absent here. The September 2026 multislices paper proves exponential lower bounds for a broad family covering known general constructions, rather than for all perfect schemes.

The upper-bound question TCS-0465 asks whether every policy admits shares with an exponent below one half. This lower-bound question asks whether some positive exponential exponent is unavoidable. Both propositions can hold simultaneously; they express different sides of the storage gap.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic communication for two-server private information retrieval
cards.formal:
Private information retrieval lets a user recover a selected database bit without revealing its index to either server. Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\), a classical one-round two-server protocol with perfect correctness and perfect privacy has total communication at most
\[
C(\log_2 n)^k
\]
bits for every database \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), requested index \(i\in[n]\), and outcome of the user's randomness? The two servers each hold the entire database and do not communicate or collude. Model & notation specifies the protocol and exact privacy requirement. There is no computational hardness assumption or bound on local computation.
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For each \(n\), a protocol specifies a nonempty finite randomness set \(\mathcal R_n\), query maps \(Q_{1,n},Q_{2,n}\), deterministic answer maps \(A_{1,n},A_{2,n}\), and a deterministic recovery map \(D_n\). Queries and answers are finite binary strings. The user samples \(r\) uniformly from \(\mathcal R_n\), independently of the database, and sends \(q_j=Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) to server \(j\). The server sends back \(a_j=A_{j,n}(x,q_j)\). There is one query and one answer per server. The user starts with only \(n,i,r\), with no database-dependent advice or shared secret.

Perfect correctness means \(D_n(i,r,a_1,a_2)=x_i\) for every \(x,i,r\). Perfect privacy means that for each \(j\in\{1,2\}\) and all \(i,i'\in[n]\), the random strings \(Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) and \(Q_{j,n}(i',r)\) have identical distributions. Since answers are deterministic functions of a server's database and query, this also protects its entire view. The servers follow the protocol; robustness to false answers and confidentiality of the rest of the database from the user are not required.

The cost is the maximum of \(|q_1|+|q_2|+|a_1|+|a_2|\) over all \(x,i,r\), where \(|w|\) is the bit length of a string \(w\). Protocol descriptions may depend on \(n\) but not on \(x\) or \(i\). There is no uniformity or local-running-time restriction. The same constants \(C,k\) must work for every database size; they cannot grow with \(n\). Answers may contain more than one bit.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a protocol family and universal constants exist, or prove the logical negation. Privacy must be exact against each computationally unbounded individual server. The bound includes both queries and both answers in the worst case. Computational privacy, database-dependent client preprocessing, or a growing number of servers changes the target.
cards.why: Can keeping the address of a requested bit completely secret cost only a polynomial in the address length? This isolates the information cost of privacy from encryption assumptions, server computation and implementation details.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
cards.why: This asks whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable total problems beyond classical randomization. It identifies the exact classical lower bound needed to turn an efficient quantum decision algorithm into an unconditional separation of computational power.

cards.context:
Quantum computation evolves complex amplitudes, whose cancellations allow interference; a final measurement gives an ordinary random bit. Both classes on this card still require reliable membership decisions on every input. Efficient classical randomized computation is contained in the quantum class. The open issue is strictness of that containment, not whether one particular classical simulation has an exponential cost.

The fixed Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT gates form a standard universal quantum basis. Boykin and coauthors establish universality for this finite set; the quarter-phase gate is exactly the T matrix in the definition. The model therefore does not supply infinitely many arbitrary gate parameters as free computational information.

Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms, with polynomial measured in the input bit length. These are function tasks. Their algorithms alone supply neither a proof that every classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm fails nor the complete total-language separation requested here. The classical hardness needed for such a separation is not a conclusion of Shor’s theorem.

Raz and Tal prove that some oracle \(O\) satisfies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^{O}\), where the polynomial hierarchy \(\mathrm{PH}\) allows any fixed number of alternating polynomially bounded existential and universal quantifiers around a polynomial-time predicate. This implies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}^{O}\). Both sides receive the same fixed black-box function, and the quantum machine may query it coherently on a superposition. The cost and power of that oracle are part of the changed model; the result does not itself separate the unrelativized classes.

Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication proves an unconditional sampling separation for shallow circuits. In Theorem 3 and Corollary 4, the classical circuits have fan-in two and at most \(n+n^\delta\) fair random inputs for fixed \(\delta<1\); approximating the stated distribution requires depth \(\Omega(\log\log n)\). Closeness is total variation distance, half the sum of absolute differences between outcome probabilities. The quantum constant-depth model permits arbitrary constant-size unitaries. These are explicit sampling and circuit-resource conditions, not an exclusion of arbitrary polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

A promise problem specifies disjoint yes and no sets and leaves other inputs unconstrained. Miloschewsky, Podder and Rudolph’s September 2026 preprint gives an oracle with \(\mathrm{BPP}^{O}=\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\) for total languages but \(\mathrm{PromiseBPP}^{O}\ne\mathrm{PromiseBQP}^{O}\). This shows, in a relativized setting, why a language equality cannot simply be substituted for the corresponding promise equality. It does not prove equality or separation of the ordinary total-language classes here.

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
cards.formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\). The classical reduction requirement preserves the saved card’s variant; the cited survey’s standard formulation permits quantum reductions.
cards.definitions:
A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\), with basis \(|0\rangle=(1,0)\) and \(|1\rangle=(0,1)\). The \(n\)-qubit state space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). A pure state is a vector of norm one; a general state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator \(\rho\) of trace one on that space. The adjoint \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(M\) is Hermitian when \(M=M^*\). The order \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N-M\) is Hermitian and \(z^*(N-M)z\geq0\) for every complex vector \(z\). The symbol \(I\) denotes the identity on the relevant space.

A local term is specified by an increasing list of \(\ell\) distinct qubit indices, with \(0\leq\ell\leq\min(k,n)\), and the complete \(2^\ell\)-by-\(2^\ell\) matrix in lexicographic computational-basis order on these indices. It acts as that matrix on the listed tensor factors and as identity on all other factors. A zero-qubit matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity. The bounds \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\) concern the embedded operator, equivalently its supplied local matrix. Different terms may overlap and need not commute. Repeated terms are allowed and counted in \(m\). No spatial geometry, bound on the number of terms touching one qubit, or common zero-energy state is required.

The ground energy is
\[\lambda_{\min}(H)=\min_{\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle
=\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}\rho=1}\operatorname{tr}(H\rho).\]
Both minima range over all global states, including entangled ones; no circuit preparation or classical description bound is imposed on a state. The promise gap \(b-a\) separates the two input cases. It is not a gap between the first and second eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian. The normalization and the per-term bound fix the energy scale, so \(0\leq\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq1\).

The input is an explicit finite bit string. To fix an encoding, for a natural number \(u\) let \(w(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(w(0)=0\), and write \(E(u)=1^{|w(u)|}0w(u)\). Encode an integer by a sign bit followed by \(E\) of its absolute value: sign 0 is nonnegative and sign 1 is negative, with sign 0 for zero. Encode a rational by its integer numerator and its positive denominator in lowest terms. A complex entry is its real rational part followed by its imaginary rational part. The instance consists of \(1^n0\), then \(E(m)\), then the rationals \(a,b\), then the \(m\) terms. A term consists of \(E(\ell)\), its \(\ell\) indices encoded by \(E\), and its matrix entries in row-major order. There are no trailing bits. The entire length \(N\) counts every numerator, denominator, index and matrix entry. Matrix precision is part of \(N\), not a unit-cost real input. Strings failing these syntactic conditions or any stated matrix or threshold condition are outside the promise, as are valid instances with \(a<\lambda_{\min}(H)<b\).

Here QMA is the following class of promise pairs \(\Pi=(Y,N_0)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). A verifier has one deterministic classical Turing machine that, given \(x\), outputs a quantum circuit \(V_x\) and its register sizes in time polynomial in \(|x|+1\). The circuit has polynomially many qubits and gates, with a designated witness register of \(w(|x|)\) qubits and all other qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\). The function \(w\) is polynomial-time computable and polynomially bounded. The generator and all resource bounds are fixed for \(\Pi\), valid on all inputs, and have no advice or oracle. The witness may be any density operator on its register and need not have an efficient description.

Circuits use the fixed gate set consisting of the Hadamard gate
\[W=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\]
the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and controlled-NOT, which sends \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin{\oplus}v\rangle\) for bits \(u,v\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates are specified by their names and qubit indices. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; outcome 1 is acceptance. Probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to the witness and zero ancillas after the circuit. For every \(x\in Y\), some witness is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in N_0\), every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). There is no acceptance requirement outside \(Y\cup N_0\).

QMA-hardness under the required reductions means that for every such pair \(\Pi\), there is one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(R_\Pi\) that halts on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^r\) bit steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,r\), outputs a classical binary string, and satisfies
\[x\in Y\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm yes},\qquad
x\in N_0\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm no}.\]
Output writing is included in the time bound. On promised source inputs the output must obey every target condition, including the common locality and term-count bounds. Off the source promise no output guarantee is required, but the runtime bound still holds. The reduction may depend on \(\Pi\); \(k,d,\varepsilon\) must be chosen once before quantifying over \(\Pi\). Thus the order is \(\exists k,d,\varepsilon\;\forall\Pi\in\mathrm{QMA}\;\exists R_\Pi\). No random or quantum computation is allowed in \(R_\Pi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full stated existence of constants and classical QMA-hardness, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must prove the reduction guarantees and their uniform polynomial resource bounds for all QMA promise pairs with one fixed target triple \((k,d,\varepsilon)\). A negative answer must establish that for every allowed triple there is a QMA promise pair admitting no qualifying classical reduction to that target problem. The source pair may depend on the triple. A lower bound on one proposed reduction, a counterexample only to a particular construction, an oracle separation, or an algorithm for a restricted Hamiltonian family is not this negation. A proof allowing only quantum reductions does not by itself prove the saved classical-reduction variant; conversely, refuting the latter need not refute the weaker standard formulation. Constant-gap hardness with growing locality, a theorem solely about preparation depth of low-energy states, or an interactive verification theorem does not meet this answer criterion.
cards.why: This asks whether coarse average-energy estimation retains the full difficulty of verification with an arbitrary quantum witness. The per-term normalization prevents a numerical rescaling from creating the required gap. A positive result would give a robust quantum analogue of classical constraint-satisfaction hardness, with consequences for the computational structure of low-energy states. The saved classical-reduction version additionally requires that the hard physical instance be produced without quantum computation.

cards.context:
Editorial scope: the existing card explicitly chose deterministic classical reductions. This review preserves that mathematical target and qualifies the title. Aharonov, Arad and Vidick instead state their Conjecture 1.3 under quantum polynomial-time reductions, and explain that permitting quantum reductions is needed for the known equivalence with their proof-verification formulation. The stronger reduction requirement here is therefore not attributed to their conjecture as an established equivalent formulation.

The classical PCP theorem gives constant-gap hardness for constraint satisfaction. Quantum local Hamiltonians replace local Boolean penalties by local operators, while a global state may be entangled across all qubits. The quantum Cook–Levin theorem establishes QMA-completeness at inverse-polynomial relative precision. The constant relative gap asked for here remains an additional claim. The no case rules out low average energy for every state, rather than only product states or a specified family of trial states.

Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe proved the no-low-energy-trivial-states theorem, first announced in 2022 and published at STOC 2023. Their families have bounded-size local interactions and a fixed positive energy-density threshold below which state preparation needs depth \(\Omega(\log n)\). Depth counts layers of disjoint bounded-size quantum gates, with no geometric restriction. This establishes a strong structural phenomenon in low-energy states, but is not a reduction proving QMA-hardness of distinguishing high and low ground energies. In particular, their theorem’s Hamiltonians are frustration-free: they have a common zero-energy state.

The games version also requires care. Natarajan and Nirkhe’s 2024 status note identifies an error in an earlier Natarajan–Vidick energy-amplification argument that invalidates its claimed games PCP for a QMA-complete problem. Their note distinguishes efficient honest provers from arbitrarily powerful entangled provers. Neither the old claim nor general results about interactive games supply the Hamiltonian statement on this card.

Buhrman, Helsen and Weggemans give a detailed quantum reduction between constant-query proof checking and local Hamiltonians, and clarify adaptive-query and multiple-prover variants. Their 2025 theorem controls approximation of a verifier’s acceptance probability by an energy and can produce a fixed classical Hamiltonian description with high probability. The reduction itself is quantum. These structural results do not establish that all QMA problems have constant-query proofs, or that the needed Hamiltonian descriptions can always be computed by classical reductions.

The October 2025 Bergamaschi–Metger–Vidick–Zhang preprint proves a gap-amplification result with an increase in the locality of the resulting Hamiltonian. Its locality-gap tradeoff does not preserve a constant locality throughout the full conjectured gap increase. Thus it is a distinct partial result even though its reductions can be deterministic.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 preprint gives interactive oracle proofs for QMA with polynomial total communication, polylogarithmic query and round counts, and a constant soundness gap. The interaction and nonconstant query bounds are part of the theorem. It does not assert the noninteractive, constant-locality Hamiltonian hardness asked for here. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Nguyen’s July 23, 2026 Simons talk abstract explicitly keeps the general quantum PCP question open and reports amplification of a combinatorial gap. The checked abstract does not assert the full normalized energy-gap theorem. A matching full paper or video proof was not verified in this review.

Bafna and Vyas’s August 19, 2026 preprint also explicitly describes quantum PCP as open. It concerns classical private PCPs for NP, with nonconstant query complexity and additional parameter improvements conditional on a product-expansion conjecture. Its classical result does not verify quantum witnesses or settle this Hamiltonian problem.

cards.title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every choice of integers \(q\ge2\), \(r,g\ge1\) and real numbers \(J,\Delta>0\), does there exist a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta)\ge0\) with the following property? For every square-lattice size \(L\ge1\), every Hamiltonian satisfying the locality, norm, incidence, unique-ground-state and global-gap conditions below, and every subset \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), its ground state satisfies \[S(\rho_A)\le C\,|\partial A|.\] The constant must be independent of \(L\), the region and the particular interaction matrices. This is an entropy area law for general uniformly gapped two-dimensional local systems.
cards.definitions:
Let \(\Lambda_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^2\), with open boundaries and a copy of \(\mathbb C^q\) at each site. The full Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_L=\bigotimes_{x\in\Lambda_L}\mathbb C^q\), with the standard product basis and inner product \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian operator \(H=\sum_a h_a\), with a finite list of Hermitian interaction terms. Each term acts as identity outside a specified nonempty support \(X_a\subseteq\Lambda_L\). Its support has diameter at most \(r\) in the maximum-coordinate distance \(d_\infty(x,y)=\max\{|x_1-y_1|,|x_2-y_2|\}\). A one-site support has diameter zero. Each site belongs to at most \(g\) listed supports; terms with equal supports are counted separately. Every term has operator norm at most \(J\), where \(\|T\|=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Tv\|\) and \(\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\). The terms need not be positive, commute, be translation invariant or admit a common energy-minimizing state.

List the eigenvalues of \(H\), with multiplicity, as \(E_0\le E_1\le\cdots\). Its lowest eigenspace is required to have dimension one and \(E_1-E_0\ge\Delta\). Choose a unit eigenvector \(\psi\) for \(E_0\). Uniqueness means uniqueness up to global phase, so \(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\) is uniquely specified. The gap condition concerns the entire Hamiltonian only. No lower gap bound is assumed for subregions or subsets of its interaction terms. Both \(J\) and \(\Delta\) are in the same fixed energy units.

For \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), let \(A^c=\Lambda_L\setminus A\) and let \(\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{A^c}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\). Partial trace is defined in product-basis indices by \[(\rho_A)_{u,v}=\sum_z\psi_{(u,z)}\,\overline{\psi_{(v,z)}},\] where \(u,v\) index basis configurations on \(A\), \(z\) ranges over configurations on \(A^c\), and tuples are placed in the original site order. This is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one. If its eigenvalues are \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_D\), its entropy in bits is \(S(\rho_A)=-\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\).

The geometric boundary \(\partial A\) consists of unordered nearest-neighbor lattice edges \(\{x,y\}\) with exactly one endpoint in \(A\), where \(|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|=1\). Its cardinality is measured in lattice units and is defined by geometry, even if a particular Hamiltonian has no term crossing an edge. No exterior vertices or periodic wrap-around edges are added. Regions may be disconnected or touch the exterior boundary. Empty and full regions have zero entropy and zero internal boundary. The interaction matrices may have arbitrary complex entries and may vary with location and with \(L\). There is no finite input encoding, state-preparation task, efficient computation requirement or frustration-free assumption. The question asks for a uniform mathematical entropy bound across all the specified finite systems.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal statement with the displayed order of quantifiers, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative answer fixes one choice of \(q,r,g,J,\Delta\) and shows that for every finite \(C\ge0\), there is an admissible system and region violating the bound. Equivalently, it may exhibit a sequence with these same fixed local parameters, unique ground states, gaps at least \(\Delta\), and unbounded ratios \(S(\rho_A)/|\partial A|\) on nontrivial regions. Allowing the gap to close, the interaction norm or local dimension to grow, or the lowest eigenspace to become degenerate does not refute this statement. A positive result for frustration-free or locally gapped systems, only one family of interactions, or an entropy bound with an unbounded extra logarithmic or subpolynomial factor does not prove it. No algorithm for finding the ground state is required. The statement is an exact yes/no bound; a fixed additive approximation to individual entropies is not a substitute.
cards.why: A central problem in quantum Hamiltonian complexity: whether locality plus a uniform gap controls the quantum information in ground states in two dimensions. It would sharpen the structural foundations of tensor-network methods and separate the task of bounding entanglement from the further task of computing the state.
