cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis, planted clique isolates a gap between statistical information and efficient computation. The hidden clique is far larger than cliques arising by chance, yet no unrestricted polynomial-time detector is established in this regime. Related assumptions support hardness results for estimation, clustering and other inference tasks. Proving this formulation would imply Boolean \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\): a polynomial-time general clique decider would distinguish these distributions once \(k_n\) exceeds the typical null clique size.

cards.context:
The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. The card retains the concrete fixed-size, balanced constant-success detection question already selected here. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving this card’s fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.

cards.title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true in the ordinary uniform Turing-machine model?
\[\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ :\ (L,D^S)\notin\mathrm{AvgP}.
\]
Here \(S\) is one exact polynomial-time sampler, \(D^S=(D^S_n)_{n\ge1}\) its output distribution ensemble, and \(\mathrm{AvgP}\) means deterministic, always-correct computation with the positive-moment runtime bound below. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language and one fixed feasible sampling procedure for which no exact deterministic decider has average polynomial running time. No additional hardness or derandomization hypothesis may be assumed.
cards.definitions:
All algorithms have one fixed finite program, use ordinary multitape Turing machines with finite tape alphabets and unit-cost transitions, and receive explicit binary strings. There is no oracle or nonuniform advice. Randomized machines obtain independent fair coin bits; reading input, generating coins, computing intermediate data and writing output all take time.

A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{P}\) if one deterministic machine decides membership on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps for fixed positive integers \(a,d\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,d\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary certificate \(y\) of length at most \(a(|x|+1)^d\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). The verifier is total and polynomial time in its full input length. The premise concerns these total decision classes.

A sampler \(S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) is one randomized machine which, on unary input \(1^n\), \(n\ge1\), halts on every random tape within \(q(n)=a(n+1)^d\) steps, for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on \(S\). It outputs a finite binary string of length at most \(q(n)\), possibly the empty string. Put \(D^S_n(x)=\Pr[S(1^n)=x]\). Sampling is exact, not an approximation, and its time bound holds for every coin sequence. The parameter \(n\) need not equal the sampled string length. These probabilities form a finite distribution: one may regard the random tape as \(q(n)\) fair bits, with unused bits ignored.

An exact decider \(A\) for \(L\) is one deterministic machine that, on the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,x)\), halts and returns \(1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for every \(n\ge1\) and every binary string \(x\), including strings of zero probability under \(D^S_n\). It cannot answer 'unknown'. Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of transitions, charged at least one step. There is no worst-case polynomial-time requirement on this decider. By definition,
\[(L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists A\ \exists\eta>0\ \exists C>0\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1:
\sum_x D^S_n(x)T_A(1^n,x)^{\eta}\le C(n+1)^k,
\]
where \(A\) must be an exact decider and \(\eta,C\) are real constants. The sum is over the finite support of \(D^S_n\). The algorithm and constants may depend on \(L,S\) but not on \(n\). Nonmembership means that for every such \(A,\eta,C,k\), some \(n\ge1\) violates the inequality. It is not necessary to violate it at every sufficiently large length.

This is the positive-moment convention for average polynomial time. It allows \(\eta\ne1\); the definition is not a bound on expected runtime itself and does not permit incorrect membership answers. The existentially selected sampler is part of the distributional problem, not input to the decider, which may have its fixed description built into its program.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication or its logical negation, under the stated uniform models and quantifiers. An affirmative result must, from \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, establish a fixed \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) and a fixed exact strict-polynomial-time sampler for which every deterministic exact decider fails every positive-moment polynomial bound. The sampler and language cannot depend on the decider being challenged. A negative result must prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) together with \((L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\) for every permitted \(L,S\); an oracle separation or a barrier for one reduction method is not that negation. A complete proof of the implication may use the premise without separately proving it. Partial improvements, an additional unproved hardness assumption, or a failure of one particular algorithm do not establish the target.
cards.why: Worst-case hardness alone does not explain whether feasible procedures can generate instances that remain difficult on average. Resolving this implication would connect the central decision-class separation to robust limits on exact computation under efficiently generated inputs.

cards.context:
Worst-case intractability only says that no single polynomial-time decider works on every input. It gives no immediate frequency statement about difficult inputs under a feasible sampler. The conclusion therefore quantifies over a language together with a fixed distribution ensemble; a different hard input chosen noncomputably at each length is not an admissible sampler.

The positive-moment definition is robust under polynomial changes in running time and machine representation. Rare long computations can affect the first moment much more strongly than a smaller positive moment. Heuristics that sometimes give a wrong answer have a different success condition from the total exact deciders required here.

Distributional completeness is available for polynomial-time samplable ensembles. It identifies problems whose average tractability would imply average tractability throughout the corresponding distributional NP class. Completeness alone does not establish that this class contains a hard problem under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Likewise, easiness under a particular familiar distribution need not reflect worst-case complexity.

Bogdanov–Trevisan show that certain nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Nonadaptive means that all oracle questions are chosen before their answers are read; the reduction must work for arbitrary oracles satisfying its average-correctness promise. This restriction concerns a proof mechanism, not the truth of the unrestricted implication.

Time-bounded description complexity asks how short a program can be while producing a given string within a prescribed time. Liu–Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case connection for a deterministic description problem under an additional exponential circuit-hardness assumption. Section 5 also gives a connection for randomized description complexity without that derandomization assumption, but still assumes worst-case hardness of that particular promise problem. Neither premise has been obtained from \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone in the inspected work.

The Liu–Pass paper uses AvgP for a promise-problem notion based on polynomial-time errorless heuristics, separately chosen for each inverse-polynomial failure threshold. This notation must not silently replace the card’s single exact decider and positive-moment bound. The source review records its specific model and hypotheses rather than inferring the requested general implication from a shared class name.

Liu–Mazor–Pass’s April 2026 results concern specific gap versions of description complexity, additional nonuniform hardness or derandomization assumptions, and conditional pseudorandom generators. Their hidden seed distribution can be inefficient to sample. Such a distribution does not meet the efficient sampling requirement in this question merely by existing.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that for every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) with \(n\ge1\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\), and every integer \(q\ge\Delta+2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper labelled \(q\)-colourings satisfies \[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^c?\] The constants must be independent of the graph, its degree and the number of colours. This retains the previously selected degree-uniform polynomial target; the time unit is one vertex update, not a sweep or a bit operation.
cards.definitions:
Let \(V(G)=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E(G)\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or parallel edges. Set \(N_G(v)=\{u:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\) and \(\Delta=\max_v|N_G(v)|\). The state space is \[\Omega_{G,q}=\{\sigma:[n]\to[q]:\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)\text{ for every }\{u,v\}\in E(G)\},\] where \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Colours are labelled and may be unused. There is no constraint on colour-class sizes, and no prescribed partial colouring or vertex-specific list. The state space is nonempty for the stated colour range.

At each discrete step, choose \(v\) uniformly from \([n]\). Given the current state \(\sigma\), form the available set \[A_\sigma(v)=[q]\setminus\{\sigma(u):u\in N_G(v)\}.\] Choose a colour uniformly from \(A_\sigma(v)\), assign it to \(v\), and leave every other vertex unchanged. The set has at least \(q-\Delta\ge2\) elements and includes the current colour; staying in the same colouring is allowed. The choices at successive steps are made from these conditional distributions. Let \(P\) be the resulting finite stochastic matrix and let \(P^t(\sigma,\tau)\) be its \(t\)-step transition probabilities, with \(P^0\) the identity matrix. The chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi(\sigma)=1/|\Omega_{G,q}|\), the uniform law on all proper labelled colourings. In this range it is irreducible and has self-loops, so that this stationary law is approached from every state.

Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\), over every proper initial colouring. Denote it by \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\). The chain is ergodic in the stated range.

A step updates one vertex. No factor of \(n\) is absorbed into the time unit, and uniform sampling from a potentially large colour set is part of the mathematical transition rule. Thus the statement concerns the convergence rate of a specified chain, not an implementation bound polynomial only in \(n\) for operations on \(\log q\)-bit colour names. If a graph is encoded for formalization, use its explicit vertex and edge lists and the binary integer \(q\); no succinct graph representation is intended.

The bound is simultaneous for all finite degrees and all \(q\ge\Delta+2\), including \(q\) unbounded as a function of \(n\). A theorem of the form \(C_{\Delta,q}n^{c_{\Delta,q}}\) for each fixed pair of parameters does not automatically meet it. No girth, treewidth, chordality, planarity, expansion or random-graph assumption is imposed. Girth is the shortest cycle length, with infinity for a forest. A fixed multiplicative slack \(q\ge(1+\delta)\Delta\), with \(\delta>0\), does not cover \(q=\Delta+2\) uniformly as \(\Delta\) increases.

The heat-bath convention differs from proposing a uniformly random colour from all \([q]\) and rejecting a conflict, often also called Glauber or Metropolis dynamics. In the heat-bath chain, every proposed colour is available; in the latter chain, unsuccessful proposals contribute further holding probability. Flip dynamics can recolour an entire two-colour component and is a third chain. Related results must retain their update convention and comparison costs. The present question fixes the heat-bath chain exactly.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed uniform polynomial bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its failure. An affirmative proof must supply absolute \(C,c\) working for every graph, degree, colour count and initial proper colouring in the definition. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(C,c\) there are eligible \(n,G,q\) with \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)>Cn^c\); one slow instance does not refute every polynomial. Polynomial mixing only for each fixed degree with an uncontrolled exponent, larger multiplicative palette slack, restricted graphs, a different dynamics, or an unspecified faster sampler is not the required bound. This is an exact asymptotic proposition about the specified chain, not a request to approximate a finite mixing time to the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: This tests whether the simplest local update rule samples proper colourings efficiently throughout the full range where it is guaranteed to move between all solutions. It connects random sampling, approximate counting and antiferromagnetic spin systems at a longstanding boundary for general graphs.

cards.context:
The source poses polynomial mixing at the degree-plus-two threshold. This card retains the already adopted heat-bath update rule and the explicit requirement of one polynomial for all degrees and palettes. The source’s initial update description uses proposal-and-rejection; that clock is stated separately rather than silently identifying its transition matrix with this one.

At one fewer colour, a clique on Δ+1 vertices can be frozen: every vertex already sees every other colour. Thus ergodicity itself can fail at q=Δ+1. At q≥Δ+2 the basic chain is ergodic, but eventual convergence alone supplies no polynomial bound on how long it takes.

The2020 source proves polynomial mixing for bounded-treewidth graphs at the additive threshold and for chordal graphs with fixed multiplicative slack. Its treewidth-dependent exponent and the extra hypotheses do not establish the all-graph uniform statement.

The2024 flip-dynamics theorem applies for Δ≥125 and q≥1.809Δ. Its comparison gives polynomial Glauber mixing in that range; the sharper O(n log n) corollary permits a constant depending on degree and palette. Neither the larger palette ratio nor that parameter dependence is the selected degree-plus-two theorem.

The August2026 girth-seven revision treats Metropolis updates with q≥(1+δ)Δ, for fixed δ and degree sufficiently large in terms of δ. The separate girth-five preprint gives a heat-bath theorem under analogous fixed-slack and large-degree conditions. The latter’s general bound is Oδ(n² log q+n log(1/ε)); its optimal-order corollary has further bounded-degree qualifications. Both retain structural assumptions absent here.

The ICALP2026 paper repeats the ordinary colouring-sampling conjecture before studying prescribed colour-class sizes. Fixing class sizes changes the stationary state space and the allowed moves, so those refined sampling results do not settle the chain defined here.

cards.title: Polynomial mixing of critical three-dimensional Ising dynamics
cards.formal:
For the zero-field nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model on the three-dimensional box \(V_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^{3}\) with free boundary conditions, at the infinite-lattice critical inverse temperature \(\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) defined below, is the worst-initial-state total-variation mixing time of random-site heat-bath dynamics polynomial in \(L\)? Precisely, do there exist constants \(C,a>0\) such that
\[\forall L\in\mathbb N,\ L\ge1,\qquad t_{\mathrm{mix}}(L,1/4)\le C(L+1)^a?\]
Time is counted in individual site-update attempts. The critical parameter is fixed independently of \(L\), and the target is the exact critical point, not a subcritical parameter approaching it at an unspecified rate.
cards.definitions:
Let \(E_L\) contain each unordered pair of vertices of \(V_L\) at lattice distance \(\|u-v\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{3}|u_i-v_i|=1\), once. A configuration is \(\sigma\in\Omega_L=\{-1,+1\}^{V_L}\). At inverse temperature \(\beta\ge0\), the Gibbs probability is
\[\pi_{L,\beta}(\sigma)=Z_{L,\beta}^{-1}\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right),\]
where \(Z_{L,\beta}\) is the sum of the displayed weight over all configurations. Each interaction strength is one, there is no external magnetic field, and free boundary means there are no interactions with vertices outside \(V_L\). Boundary vertices inside the box are updated just like other vertices.

To specify the critical inverse temperature without a numerical approximation, let \(B_R=\{-R,\ldots,R\}^{3}\subset\mathbb Z^3\), for integers \(R\ge1\). Define \(\mu^+_{R,\beta}\) on spins in \(B_R\) by fixing all neighboring exterior spins to \(+1\): its weight is proportional to
\[\exp\!\left(\beta\left[\sum_{\substack{\{u,v\}\subset B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\sigma_v+\sum_{\substack{u\in B_R,\ v\notin B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\right]\right).\]
Internal unordered edges and crossing edges are each counted once. Set
\[m_+(\beta)=\inf_{R\ge1}\mathbb E_{\mu^+_{R,\beta}}[\sigma_0],\qquad\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)=\inf\{\beta\ge0:m_+(\beta)>0\}.\]
The monotone limit of finite-volume plus-boundary magnetizations gives this standard infinite-lattice critical value, which is finite and positive. Plus boundaries are used only in defining the infinite-volume threshold; the finite chain being tested has free boundaries.

In one discrete step, choose a vertex \(v\) uniformly from the \(L^3\) sites, independently of previous choices. With \(h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\), redraw its spin as \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-\beta h_v(\sigma))},\]
and as \(-1\) otherwise, leaving all other spins unchanged. Choosing its existing value still counts as one step. Set \(\beta=\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) and denote the resulting transition matrix by \(P_L\). This finite chain is irreducible and aperiodic and has stationary measure \(\pi_L=\pi_{L,\beta_c}\).

Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\) for \(P_L\) with law \(\pi_L\), from every initial spin configuration. One step is one site update. A continuous-time clock of rate one per site has a different normalization. The target concerns the defined transition law with its exact probabilities.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the polynomial mixing bound or its negation for this exact model. A positive proof must establish finite constants independent of \(L\), with the critical parameter, free boundaries, update rule, worst initial state and distance threshold specified here. A negative proof must show that no fixed polynomial bounds this sequence of mixing times. Results at a tree threshold, in another lattice dimension, below criticality, with different boundaries or from a restricted initialization do not meet the criterion.
cards.why: This is a basic question about whether a standard local sampling dynamics remains efficient at a phase transition in three dimensions. The equilibrium system has correlations on many scales, so high-temperature mixing guarantees do not directly apply. A polynomial bound or a superpolynomial obstruction would clarify the computational cost of critical fluctuations in one of the central lattice models.

cards.title: FP versus #P
cards.formal:
Is every function in \(\#\mathrm{P}\) computable exactly in deterministic polynomial time? With the numerical function convention defined below, the proposition is
\[\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N},\]
equivalently \(\#\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). Each function may have its own fixed machine and polynomial running-time bound. The output is the exact nonnegative integer in binary.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\{0,1\}^*\) for all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) for their bit length. Natural numbers include zero. A polynomial witness bound is a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients; allowing any polynomial-time computable, polynomially bounded integer length gives the same class by unique zero padding. A verifier \(V(x,y)\) is a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine returning a bit on every pair of strings within polynomially many bit steps in \(|x|+|y|\). The class \(\#\mathrm{P}\) consists of the total functions
\[f_{V,p}(x)=\left|\left\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\right\}\right|.\]
Each distinct witness string is counted once. If several witnesses describe the same combinatorial object, their multiplicity is retained. The witness length is exactly the displayed length; shorter witnesses are not additionally counted. Equivalently, these functions count accepting paths of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines with binary choices and an explicit machine convention preserving path counts.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to nonnegative integers for which some deterministic multitape Turing machine outputs the canonical binary representation on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps. Here \(C,d\) are fixed positive integers, the representation of zero is the single bit 0, and positive outputs have no leading zeros. All computation and output writing are charged. Machines have finite programs, no advice and no oracle. No error probability or approximation is allowed. The constants and program may depend on the function but never on the input. There is no requirement of a common exponent or a uniform compiler taking arbitrary verifiers as input.

Every \(\#\mathrm{P}\) value is at most \(2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has at most \(p(|x|)+1\) bits. The question does not request output in unary, listing all witnesses, or a time bound polynomial in the value of the count. Conversely, if a numerical function has a polynomial-time exact algorithm, choose a polynomial \(q\) longer than its output bit bound and accept a \(q(|x|)\)-bit witness precisely when its numerical value is smaller than \(f(x)\). Exactly \(f(x)\) witnesses are accepted. Thus \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm{P}\), which justifies writing equality rather than only the displayed inclusion. The source writes FP for this numerical interpretation of polynomial-time string functions.

For the comparisons below, \(\mathrm{P}\) is the class of languages decided by deterministic machines in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages of the form \(\{x:f_{V,p}(x)>0\}\). Use the shared definition of [PSPACE](definitions.html#space). A polynomial-time Turing reduction to a numerical function may make adaptively chosen exact queries, charging query writing and answer processing, while receiving the binary answer from its oracle. Counting completeness mentioned below uses this convention unless a stronger count-preserving reduction is stated.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\), or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must supply existence of an exact uniform polynomial-time machine for every fixed verifier and witness bound; it suffices to solve an appropriately proved counting-complete problem exactly in polynomial time. A negative proof must establish a \(\#\mathrm{P}\) function admitting no such machine. A conditional separation assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), a lower bound for one restricted algorithm, or an efficient relative approximation does not by itself settle the unconditional proposition. Computing only whether the count is zero is also insufficient.
cards.why: This is the fundamental exact-counting analogue of P versus NP. It asks whether every efficiently checkable family of witnesses also admits efficient evaluation of its full multiplicity, and connects counting satisfiability, permanents and many discrete partition functions under one computational boundary.

cards.context:
A verifier checks one proposed witness quickly. Its counting function asks how many witnesses pass. The count can be exponentially large while its binary representation remains polynomially short, so the difficulty is not simply the time needed to write the answer.

Exact counting immediately decides whether any witness exists. Consequently, an affirmative answer implies P = NP, and a proof that P differs from NP would give a negative answer here. The converse implication is a separate question: efficient existence tests do not automatically evaluate the full count.

Counting satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula is a representative complete problem. The usual verifier-to-formula construction can retain one satisfying assignment per accepted witness by forcing the values of auxiliary computation variables. Therefore a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm for those formulas would evaluate every function in the class.

Some counting-complete problems have easy existence tests. For a zero-one matrix, its permanent counts perfect matchings in the associated bipartite graph; testing whether such a matching exists is polynomial-time solvable. Counting completeness here is under polynomial-time oracle reductions, and does not mean a count-preserving reduction from satisfiability.

This stronger hypothesis is distinct from P = NP, and the brute-force counting procedure itself generally takes exponential time.

Relative approximation allows a nonzero error proportional to the count. When the count is exponential, even a very small inverse-polynomial relative error can hide many integers. An approximation algorithm whose running time is polynomial in inverse accuracy can need exponential time at the precision that distinguishes adjacent counts.

cards.title: FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every finite undirected simple graph \(G\) and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(A(G,\varepsilon)\) halts on every random tape within
\[C\bigl(N+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) satisfying
\[\Pr\bigl[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\bigr]\ge\frac34?\]
Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of perfect matchings, \(N\) is the complete input bit length defined below, and, whenever \(Z(G)=0\), every run must output zero. This is the existence question for a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme on general unweighted graphs.
cards.definitions:
For every integer \(n\ge0\), a graph has labeled vertex set \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and an arbitrary subset of the unordered pairs of distinct vertices as its edges. It has no loops, parallel edges or weights. A matching is a subset of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints; it is perfect when every vertex is incident to exactly one of its edges. Each such edge set is counted once, regardless of order or orientation. Thus \(Z(G)\in\mathbb N\), an odd-order graph has count zero, and the empty graph has count one, from its empty matching. The domain includes disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles and arbitrarily large degrees, with no bipartiteness, density, planarity, expansion, or existence promise.

Use the following explicit finite encoding. The graph is encoded by \(1^{n}0\) followed by one adjacency bit for each pair \(0\le i<j<n\), in lexicographic order. This includes the full vertex set even when there are no edges and is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. Write \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms with integers \(0<r<s\). Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Append \(E(r)E(s)\) to the graph encoding. The total length is \(N\); the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\), not just the length of its encoding, may enter the time bound. The output has the form \(E(u)E(v)\) with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), meaning \(\widehat Z=u/v\); reduction to lowest terms is not required.

An algorithm is one finite multitape probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, and an output tape. Each ordinary transition and each newly requested independent fair bit costs one step. Its probability space is the infinite product of fair bits, and the clock bound must hold on every tape for every valid input. Reading, arithmetic, storage operations and writing the whole rational output are all charged. There is no advice, oracle, nonuniform dependence on the graph or accuracy, or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers. No guarantee is needed on malformed inputs. The same \(A,C,k\) must work for all graphs and all valid accuracies; success is per input and is not an average over a graph distribution.

The estimate has relative multiplicative error. In particular, an additive error guarantee on the raw count or on its logarithm is a different condition. Requiring deterministic zero output when no perfect matching exists is a harmless normalization of the usual FPRAS question because perfect-matching existence on general graphs is deterministically decidable in polynomial time. The probability \(3/4\) is fixed, and no random output is required to be an actual matching. This card asks whether the approximation algorithm exists; it does not ask for the numerical value of a fixed graph’s count at the catalogue’s default absolute tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition above or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite uniform algorithm and constants \(C,k\), and prove its every-random-tape clock, output encoding, exact zero behavior and per-input relative-error probability for every graph and rational accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm and every such polynomial bound; it need not consist of a single finite counterexample graph. Failure or slow mixing of a particular algorithm family does not prove that negation. A conditional impossibility theorem is only a conditional result unless its hypothesis is also proved. Exact exponential-time counting, constant-factor approximation without arbitrary requested accuracy, algorithms only for bipartite or dense graphs, and approximation of the total number of all matchings do not meet the target.
cards.why: A canonical unresolved problem in approximate counting, separating efficient existence testing from estimating the number of solutions. It also controls the approximability of other counting and partition-function problems through reductions.

cards.context:
Finding a perfect matching is possible in deterministic polynomial time on general graphs, but exact counting is #P-complete even on bipartite graphs. A relative approximation can be much easier than exact counting, as the permanent demonstrates. This question asks whether that distinction persists on all simple graphs, making it one of the central missing cases in the theory of randomized approximate counting.

For an \(m\times m\) nonnegative matrix \(B\), its permanent is \(\operatorname{per}(B)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}B_{i,\pi(i)}\), where \(S_{m}\) is the set of permutations. When \(B\) is a zero–one bipartite adjacency matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings between the two specified vertex classes. Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda prove an FPRAS for every nonnegative permanent, solving the bipartite matching case. Their theorem does not require the matrix entries to be strictly positive.

For a general graph on an even number of vertices, the corresponding expression is the hafnian of its symmetric adjacency matrix: the sum, over partitions of the vertices into unordered pairs, of the product of the selected entries. It is different from the permanent of that same square matrix. For example, \(K_{4}\) has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine, because the latter also counts directed cycle covers. This example identifies the mathematical distinction between the two targets.

Jerrum and Sinclair’s 1989 Corollary 4.5 gives an FPRAS for the number of matchings of all sizes in arbitrary unweighted graphs. The related weighted monomer–dimer statement has a weight-encoding qualification; no unrestricted binary-weight theorem is needed here. Total matching count can differ exponentially from perfect-matching count: a disjoint union of \(j\) edges has \(2^{j}\) matchings but only one perfect matching. Thus the two quantities are not interchangeable even on elementary graphs.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes identify a precise obstruction for a family of chains on perfect and near-perfect matchings. A near-perfect matching leaves exactly two vertices uncovered, and its hole pattern records those vertices. For the specified JSV-type transitions and any weighting depending only on the hole pattern, their Theorem 2.2 gives graphs on which either perfect matchings have exponentially small stationary probability or the mixing time is exponential. The disjunction matters: the theorem does not assert slow mixing for every weighting, nor impossibility of every FPRAS. Their positive result treats bounded ear complexity of factor-critical subgraphs; a factor-critical graph remains perfectly matchable after deleting any one vertex, and ear count is not its vertex count.

The relevance extends to statistical counting models. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s Proposition 1.2 recalls that, for fixed rational equal interaction parameters \(\beta=\gamma<-1\), approximation of the corresponding two-state spin partition function is equivalent to general perfect-matching approximation under reductions preserving the existence of an FPRAS. The source states this equivalence in both directions and explicitly identifies the perfect-matching question as open. Its other tractable parameter regimes therefore do not settle this one.

Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s preprint of 27 August 2026 reports an improved permanent FPRAS. For an \(m\times m\) zero–one matrix with \(m\ge2\), its Theorem 1 states time \(O(m^{6}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{5}m\log(2/\delta))\) for relative error \(\varepsilon\) and failure probability \(\delta\); the trivial and zero-permanent cases are handled separately. The state space remains bipartite. This is a reported preprint running-time improvement within the solved neighboring case, not a general-graph theorem; its full proof and bit-level implementation were not independently verified here.

Zihong Yi’s preprint of 3 September 2026 claims a deterministic approximation scheme for weighted hafnians when the support graph has minimum degree at least \((1/2+\gamma)n\) and nonzero weights lie in \([\theta,1]\), for fixed \(\gamma>0\) and \(\theta>0\). The unweighted case takes \(\theta=1\), but it still has the fixed density margin. The polynomial’s exponents depend on these fixed margins. The paper explicitly retains the general nonbipartite FPRAS question as open and separately discusses its limitations at the exact Dirac threshold. The reviewed statement does not cover every graph, and the full new proof has not been independently verified.

A positive answer would extend a landmark success of randomized counting beyond bipartiteness. A negative answer would establish a separation between the ease of finding these objects and the existence of arbitrarily accurate relative estimates of their number. The source-specific Markov-chain obstruction explains part of the difficulty without deciding this algorithm-independent question.

cards.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every integer \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and every integer \(t\ge1\), if \(\chi(G)\ge t\), then \(G\) contains \(K_t\) as an ordinary graph minor. Equivalently, \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every such graph, where \(h\) is the Hadwiger number defined below.
cards.definitions: The edge set of \(G\) is any set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices in \([n]\); there are no loops or parallel edges. For an integer \(r\ge1\), a proper \(r\)-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(r\); it exists and lies between \(1\) and \(n\). The graph \(K_t\) has \(t\) vertices and every possible edge. A \(K_t\) minor in \(G\) means that there are \(t\) pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) with both of the following properties: for every \(i\), any two vertices of \(B_i\) are joined by a finite path of edges of \(G\) whose vertices all lie in \(B_i\); and for every \(i<j\), some edge of \(G\) has one endpoint in \(B_i\) and one in \(B_j\). A singleton is connected. The branch sets may have any sizes, need not cover all vertices, and have no restrictions on extra internal edges or on parity. This is equivalent to obtaining \(K_t\) by vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions, discarding loops and merging parallel edges after contraction. It is neither an induced-minor nor an odd-minor requirement. The Hadwiger number \(h(G)\) is the largest \(t\) admitting these branch sets, so \(1\le h(G)\le n\). For \(t\ge2\), the proposition equivalently says that absence of a \(K_t\) minor implies a proper \((t-1)\)-coloring; the \(t=1\) assertion holds automatically for a nonempty graph. Relabeling vertices has no effect. The quantifiers impose no connectedness, degree, order or other restriction on \(G\), and no running-time bound on finding a coloring or a minor.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition for all finite nonempty simple undirected graphs and all integers \(t\ge1\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: existence of a finite graph \(G\) and integer \(t\ge1\) with \(\chi(G)\ge t\) and no \(t\) branch sets satisfying the definition. A counterexample must certify both the chromatic lower bound and absence of the ordinary clique minor. A proof of \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every graph is an equivalent positive answer. No efficient algorithm is required. A constant-factor or asymptotic coloring bound, a finite list of established values of \(t\), a restricted graph class, or a counterexample only to the odd-minor variant does not cover the target.
cards.why: Hadwiger’s conjecture proposes an exact relation between two basic graph parameters: the number of colors needed and the size of a complete graph obtainable by contraction. It extends the Four-Color Theorem and would turn exclusion of a complete minor into the sharp universal coloring bound. Its significance comes from this structural connection across all finite graphs, rather than from an algorithmic requirement in the question.

references.title: Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture
references.authors: Marcus Kühn; Lisa Sauermann; Raphael Steiner; Yuval Wigderson
references.locator: Version 1, 23 December 2025; full PDF §1, ordinary Conjecture 1.1 on page 1, branch-tree odd-minor definition, Conjecture 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 on page 2. Still sole arXiv version on 14 September 2026; construction proof not independently certified.

cards.context:
A complete minor can be much larger than any complete subgraph: contraction groups connected regions into single vertices. Hadwiger asks whether the resulting complete graph can always have as many vertices as the original graph needs colors. For every \(t\ge2\), the graph \(K_{t-1}\) has no \(K_t\) minor and needs exactly \(t-1\) colors, so the conjectured bound for the excluded-minor class is sharp.

The exact cases through \(t=6\) are known. The \(t=5\) case is equivalent, via Wagner’s theorem, to the Four-Color Theorem for planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas established the \(t=6\) case: without assuming four-colorability, their structural result makes a minimal counterexample apex, meaning that deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. The Four-Color Theorem then gives five colors for that graph. Their paper indexes the conjecture by the allowed number of colors, one less than the clique-minor order used on this card.

Kostochka and Thomason obtained an \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) bound on degeneracy, where a graph is \(d\)-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most \(d\). Such a graph is \((d+1)\)-colorable. The order of this degeneracy bound is tight, but that fact is not a chromatic lower bound of the same order and does not disprove Hadwiger. Delcourt and Postle’s Theorem 1.5 gives \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors for arbitrary \(K_t\)-minor-free graphs; its quantification has no bound on the number of vertices.

Liu and Luo’s version 2, submitted on 9 September 2026, states in Theorem 1.1 that an absolute constant \(C\) satisfies \(\chi(G)\le Ct\log\log\log t\) for every integer \(t\ge16\) and every \(K_t\)-minor-free graph. Their logarithms are natural. This is recorded as a recent preprint claim whose proof has not been independently verified here. It does not establish either the weakening \(\chi(G)=O(t)\) or the exact bound \(t-1\); the introduction still identifies clique-minor orders starting at seven as open.

For the odd-minor variant, the disjoint branch trees must each have a proper two-coloring, with an edge joining vertices of the same color between every pair of trees. Forgetting these extra requirements yields an ordinary minor, so absence of an ordinary minor implies absence of an odd minor; the reverse implication need not hold. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s December 2025 preprint states that for each fixed \(\delta>0\) and every sufficiently large \(t\), some graph has no odd \(K_t\) minor and has \(\chi(G)\ge(3/2-\delta)t\). This refutes the stronger odd-minor conjecture. Odd-minor absence by itself does not certify the ordinary-minor absence required for a negative answer here.

Hadwiger asks whether the resulting complete graph can always have as many vertices as the original graph needs colors. For every \(t\ge2\), the graph \(K_{t-1}\) has no \(K_t\) minor and needs exactly \(t-1\) colors, so the conjectured bound for the excluded-minor class is sharp.

The exact cases through \(t=6\) are known. The \(t=5\) case is equivalent, via Wagner’s theorem, to the Four-Color Theorem for planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas established the \(t=6\) case: without assuming four-colorability, their structural result makes a minimal counterexample apex, meaning that deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. The Four-Color Theorem then gives five colors for that graph. Their paper indexes the conjecture by the allowed number of colors, one less than the clique-minor order used on this card.

Kostochka and Thomason obtained an \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) bound on degeneracy, where a graph is \(d\)-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most \(d\). Such a graph is \((d+1)\)-colorable. The order of this degeneracy bound is tight, but that fact is not a chromatic lower bound of the same order and does not disprove Hadwiger. Delcourt and Postle’s Theorem 1.5 gives \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors for arbitrary \(K_t\)-minor-free graphs; its quantification has no bound on the number of vertices.

Liu and Luo’s version 2, submitted on 9 September 2026, states in Theorem 1.1 that an absolute constant \(C\) satisfies \(\chi(G)\le Ct\log\log\log t\) for every integer \(t\ge16\) and every \(K_t\)-minor-free graph. Their logarithms are natural. This is recorded as a recent preprint claim whose proof has not been independently verified here. It does not establish either the weakening \(\chi(G)=O(t)\) or the exact bound \(t-1\); the introduction still identifies clique-minor orders starting at seven as open.

For the odd-minor variant, the disjoint branch trees must each have a proper two-coloring, with an edge joining vertices of the same color between every pair of trees. Forgetting these extra requirements yields an ordinary minor, so absence of an ordinary minor implies absence of an odd minor; the reverse implication need not hold. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s December 2025 preprint states that for each fixed \(\delta>0\) and every sufficiently large \(t\), some graph has no odd \(K_t\) minor and has \(\chi(G)\ge(3/2-\delta)t\). This refutes the stronger odd-minor conjecture. Odd-minor absence by itself does not certify the ordinary-minor absence required for a negative answer here.

cards.status_note: The ordinary Hadwiger conjecture is explicitly open in Liu–Luo v2 of 9 September 2026, still its latest arXiv version on 14 September. Its triple-logarithmic coloring theorem is a recent preprint claim, not independently verified here. The December 2025 disproof and its September 2026 citation concern the stronger odd-minor version. Checked source formulations and a bounded later-work search do not certify all cited proofs.

cards.title: Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
cards.formal: For each integer \(h\ge 2\) and each undirected simple graph \(H\) on \([h]\), is there a real constant \(c_H>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every undirected simple graph \(G\) on \([n]\) containing no induced copy of \(H\), \[\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}\ge n^{c_H}?\] The exponent is chosen after the entire forbidden graph \(H\) and before the host graph \(G\); the assertion must hold for all such \(H\).
cards.definitions: Write \([m]=\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}\). A simple undirected graph on \([m]\) is a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation on this set; it has no loops or multiple edges. An induced copy of \(H\) in \(G\) is an injection \(f:[h]\to[n]\) such that \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent in \(H\) if and only if \(f(u)\) and \(f(v)\) are adjacent in \(G\), for every distinct \(u,v\in[h]\). Both edges and nonedges must be preserved. A clique is a vertex subset in which every distinct pair is adjacent, and an independent or stable set is one in which every distinct pair is nonadjacent. The integers \(\omega(G)\) and \(\alpha(G)\) are their respective maximum cardinalities; a homogeneous set in this card means a clique or an independent set. The right side \(n^{c_H}\) is an ordinary positive-real power, and the integer on the left is compared as a real number. The constant \(c_H\) may depend on all of \(H\), but not on \(G\) or \(n\). There is no additional degree, density, dimension or algorithmic promise. All positive host sizes, including \(n<h\), are included. This is an existence statement, with no required algorithm for computing \(c_H\) or finding the homogeneous set. A hereditary graph class is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs; a proper such class omits some finite graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer proves existence of a positive exponent for every finite forbidden graph and the homogeneous-set guarantee for every permitted host graph. A negative answer proves that there is one fixed graph \(H\) with \(|V(H)|\ge2\) such that, for every real \(c>0\), some positive integer \(n\) and some \(H\)-free graph \(G\) on \([n]\) satisfy \(\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}<n^c\). The witness host graph may depend on \(c\), but the forbidden graph must be the same for all \(c\). Failure of one proposed exponent or verification of finitely many host sizes does not establish this negation. No numerical approximation to an optimal exponent is being requested.
cards.why: This central conjecture asks whether every proper hereditary restriction forces a polynomial-size clique or independent set, far beyond the logarithmic scale possible in arbitrary graphs. It would provide a common structural guarantee across all forbidden-induced-subgraph classes and clarify the relation between local exclusions, large nearly uniform vertex sets and neighborhood complexity. These are basic objects in structural and algorithmic graph theory; the assertion itself is an existence theorem, not an efficient clique or independent-set algorithm.

cards.context:
Ramsey theory guarantees homogeneous sets on the logarithmic scale in arbitrary graphs, and random graphs show that a polynomial guarantee is impossible without restrictions. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asks whether excluding any one fixed induced pattern always changes that scale to \(n^{c_H}\) for some positive constant. A proper hereditary class omits a graph \(H\) and hence every induced copy of it, so the conjecture is equivalently a polynomial homogeneous-set guarantee for every proper hereditary class.

The conjecture is traced to 1977 in the checked modern primary papers, and Erdős and Hajnal developed it in their 1989 Ramsey-type paper. Their general bound is \(2^{a_H\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) for a suitable positive constant. Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improved this to \(2^{b_H\sqrt{\log_2 n\,\log_2\log_2 n}}\) for all \(n\ge2\). Their journal article appeared online on 6 May 2024. This still has a sublinear exponent in \(\log_2 n\) and does not yield a fixed positive power of \(n\).

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour proved the conjecture for the five-vertex path \(P_5\), whose only edges join consecutive vertices of a path. The preprint began in December 2023; the checked accepted revision is from 23 February 2026, and the journal publication is dated 23 March 2026. Together with the earlier bull and five-cycle cases and the known preservation properties, it completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices. The theorem concerns every \(P_5\)-free graph, with one positive exponent independent of its size.

The separate all-path theorem gives the following weaker guarantee: for every fixed path \(P\) and every real \(d\) with \(0<d<1\), there is \(a_{P,d}>0\) such that every \(P\)-free graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices has a homogeneous set of size at least \(2^{a_{P,d}(\log_2 n)^d}\). The constant can depend on both the path and \(d\). This explains the source notation \(2^{(\log n)^{1-o(1)}}\); its assertion for all fixed \(d<1\) does not include the required fixed-power case \(d=1\).

The 31 August 2026 revision by Huang, Ju and Zhou reports two further six-vertex cases. Both can be specified using the path \(a-b-c-d-e\) and a sixth vertex \(f\): the E-graph adds only \(cf\), while the Bird adds only \(bf\) and \(cf\). These definitions match Figures 4 and 5 of that revision. Each forbidden graph contains an induced \(P_5\), so its exclusion allows a larger host class than excluding \(P_5\). Theorems 1.10 and 1.11 concern these particular patterns, not every six-vertex graph.

Tran and Nguyen posted a further case on 28 August 2026. Their forbidden graph has vertex set \(\{a,b,c,d,e,f\}\) and exactly the edges \(\{ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df\}\); Theorem 1.1 states its Erdős–Hajnal property. It is distinct from both the E-graph and the Bird. The checked introduction still describes the general conjecture as open. The complete proofs of this preprint and the two cases in the preceding paragraph were not independently verified in this review.

Bucić, Fox and Pham prove, for each fixed forbidden graph, equivalence with two polynomial quantitative properties. The polynomial Rödl property requires that for every \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), an \(H\)-free graph on \(n\) vertices contain at least \(\varepsilon^{C_H}n\) vertices inducing edge density at most \(\varepsilon\) or at least \(1-\varepsilon\), for a fixed positive \(C_H\). The polynomial Nikiforov property permits a polynomially small proportion of induced copies of \(H\) instead of none. Their Theorem 4 proves the equivalence of these properties with Erdős–Hajnal; it does not establish any of them for every graph.

A July 2026 preprint of Sun, Wang and Zeng sharpens a result under an extra neighborhood restriction. For a graph \(G\), the open-neighborhood family is \(\{N_G(v):v\in V(G)\}\). It shatters \(S\subseteq V(G)\) if every \(A\subseteq S\) equals \(N_G(v)\cap S\) for some vertex \(v\); VC-dimension is the maximum size of a shattered set. Theorem 1.2 reports an absolute \(C\ge1\) such that dimension at most an integer \(d\ge1\) ensures a homogeneous set of size at least \(n^{(Cd)^{-d}}\). This improves the exponent in a previously proved bounded-dimension theorem. General \(H\)-free hosts in this card have no such dimension bound. The new proof was checked for scope, not independently certified.

Sági claims the full conjecture in Theorem 3.20 of the revision listed as arXiv v3, submitted 18 August 2017. The arXiv history records withdrawal of the earlier proof on 24 July 2017, and the author explicitly acknowledges a serious error in the 2012 version while offering different technical details in the revision. The withdrawal therefore cannot itself be treated as a refutation of v3. The revised full proof has not been verified here, while the checked 2026 primary literature continues to treat the general conjecture as open. This card is marked uncertain to record that unresolved proof claim accurately.

cards.title: Deterministic Exact Matching
cards.formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with an even number \(n\ge0\) of vertices, every red-edge subset \(R\subseteq E\), and every integer \(0\le k\le n/2\), the machine halts within \(K(N+1)^d\) steps and outputs YES exactly when
\[
 \exists M\subseteq E:\qquad
 \bigl(\forall v\in V,\ |\{e\in M:v\in e\}|=1\bigr)
 \quad\text{and}\quad |M\cap R|=k?
\]
Here \(N\) is the input bit length under the explicit encoding below. No bipartition is promised.
cards.definitions:
Vertices are labelled \(1,\ldots,n\), and an edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Loops and parallel edges are excluded. Every edge is either red, meaning it belongs to \(R\), or blue, meaning it belongs to \(E\setminus R\). The graph, all its edges and their colours are given explicitly, not through an oracle or a succinct circuit. One fixed encoding uses a length-prefixed binary header and a list of adjacency records, one for each vertex including isolated vertices, with neighbour labels and colour bits; each undirected edge has consistent entries at both endpoints. The integer \(k\) is in binary. The encoding contains all \(n\) vertex records, so its length is at least \(n\); a binary header alone does not describe exponentially many unlisted vertices.

A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share a vertex. It is perfect if every vertex belongs to one of its edges, equivalently the degree condition in the formula. Every perfect matching then has \(n/2\) edges. The requested count is exactly \(k\) red edges, rather than at least \(k\), at most \(k\) or a count congruent to \(k\) modulo an integer. On the empty graph, the empty matching is perfect and the allowed input \(k=0\) has answer YES.

The machine is one uniform finite classical multitape Turing program; all bit operations, reading, auxiliary computation and output count toward its running time. It has no random bits, nonuniform advice or external oracle. The same \(A,K,d\) must work on every input size, colour pattern and allowed \(k\), with no error. Malformed encodings, odd vertex counts and out-of-range values of \(k\) can be rejected as invalid inputs in polynomial time. The graph may be disconnected, nonplanar and nonbipartite, with arbitrary degrees.

The required output is a decision bit; computing the number of matchings is not requested. Polynomial time means membership of this explicitly encoded decision language in the class \(\mathrm{P}\). Only sequential polynomial time is sought; a polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithm is not required. The statement is unconditional: no computational hardness or derandomization assumption is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the stated deterministic algorithm and common polynomial bound exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof that this decision language does not belong to \(\mathrm{P}\).

A positive answer must cover both YES and NO instances on all finite simple graphs. A randomized polynomial-time procedure, nonuniform circuit family, special graph class, exact-parity test or algorithm with a small red-count or matching-size error does not by itself suffice. A conditional lower bound or a barrier to one algebraic approach is not an unconditional negative answer. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.
cards.why: Determine whether randomness can be removed from a basic exact constraint on perfect matching. The problem connects combinatorial derandomization with algebraic algorithms while keeping a short, directly checkable input and feasibility condition.

cards.context:
An ordinary perfect matching covers every vertex once. The exact colour constraint asks for one specified attainable count, which is not determined merely by optimizing the count upward or downward.

On a six-cycle whose edge colours alternate red and blue, the two perfect matchings have zero and three red edges. Counts one and two are absent even though they lie between the minimum and maximum. This elementary obstruction already occurs on bipartite inputs.

Randomized methods place the problem among natural candidates for studying the power of randomness in efficient computation. A matching witnesses a YES answer, but the target requires a deterministic polynomial-time decision on NO instances as well.

The August 2026 revision tests all red counts simultaneously in matrix-multiplication time measured in finite-field operations. Its decision algorithm still uses randomness, and the introduction explicitly leaves derandomization open.

The April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic algorithm only for bipartite graphs. Its Appendix A records eight unproved structural inputs in the Lean formalization. This review does not certify those inputs or the full proof; even a verified bipartite theorem would require a further general-graph argument to settle this card.

Randomized methods place the problem among natural candidates for studying the power of randomness in efficient computation. A matching witnesses a YES answer, but the target requires a deterministic polynomial-time decision on NO instances as well.

The August 2026 revision tests all red counts simultaneously in matrix-multiplication time measured in finite-field operations. Its decision algorithm still uses randomness, and the introduction explicitly leaves derandomization open.

The April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic algorithm only for bipartite graphs. Its Appendix A records eight unproved structural inputs in the Lean formalization. This review does not certify those inputs or the full proof; even a verified bipartite theorem would require a further general-graph argument to settle this card.

cards.title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized sequential word-RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph \(G\), terminates almost surely, always outputs a valid matching when it terminates, and outputs a maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\), with expected running time
\[(n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?\]
Here \(n=|V(G)|\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and the precise machine, input, probability and asymptotic conventions are below. In particular, the same program must meet every positive exponent slack; an algorithm chosen separately for each fixed slack is not the stated target.
cards.definitions:
Graph and optimum. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles, the empty graph and the edgeless graph are included. Put \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). A matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E\) such that no vertex belongs to two selected edges. Its cardinality is \(|M|\), and
\[\nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\]
The empty matching is allowed, so this finite maximum exists on every input. The problem is unweighted. The algorithm must return the selected edges, not only the number \(\nu(G)\), a fractional solution, or a certificate that a perfect matching exists. Any maximum matching is acceptable.

Explicit representation. Use an edge list with headers \(n,m\), the vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), and then \(m\) indexed pairs \((u_j,v_j)\) with \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and no repeated pair. Edge indices are \(j=1,\ldots,m\); their order is arbitrary. Each integer occupies one machine word, so the entire input has \(2+n+2m\) words. Isolated vertices count in \(n\). The graph is a full list, not a succinct circuit or query oracle. The output consists of its cardinality \(t\) and a list of \(t\) distinct valid edge indices, in any order. Ordinary explicit adjacency lists can be converted to this form in \(O(n+m)\) word operations, preserving the target time scale. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

Machine. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\) and, on inputs of size parameter \(N\), uses words of exactly
\[w=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits. A word represents an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of word registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially all zero. The input is read-only and the output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction operates on a constant number of words. Reading or writing an addressed word, copying, comparing, branching, bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT, and arithmetic addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\) cost one operation. Integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor also cost one operation. A left or right shift by fewer than \(w\) positions discards bits outside the word and fills with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger exact integers use multiple words, and their processing is charged. A random instruction supplies one fresh uniform \(w\)-bit word, independent of all previous random words. There are no exact-real primitives, oracle calls, nonuniform advice, or precomputed tables supplied at no cost. The program may use \(w\) as the machine word length. Preprocessing, input access, initialization it performs and writing every output word are included in time.

Randomness and correctness. For a fixed valid input, the probability space is the infinite sequence of independent uniform random words used by the machine. Let \(T_A(G,R)\) count its operations, with value \(+\infty\) on a nonterminating execution. For every input, termination must have probability one. On every terminating execution, including those outside the success event, the output indices must represent a matching. On each input separately,
\[\Pr_R[\text{the output matching has cardinality }\nu(G)]\ge2/3.\]
The output may be suboptimal on other executions, but it must remain feasible. No distribution over input graphs is assumed, and success is not merely an expectation bound on matching size. A single program is used for every graph and edge-list order.

Almost-linear expected time. The expectation is over the algorithm's random words, with the input fixed. The notation in the question means that this same algorithm and word constant satisfy
\[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \exists N_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G\text{ with }N\ge N_\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_R[T_A(G,R)]\le C_\varepsilon N^{1+\varepsilon}.\]
Constants and the threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and on the fixed algorithm, but not on the graph, its density, its edge order or its random choices. The slack \(\varepsilon\) is not an input selecting a different program. This is a worst-case-over-inputs bound on expected time, not a bound on every individual random execution. The claim covers sparse and dense graphs simultaneously and allows subpolynomial overhead beyond polylogarithmic factors.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a uniform finite program and a fixed word constant, prove almost-sure termination and feasibility on every terminating execution, prove per-input success probability at least \(2/3\), and establish the displayed expected-time bound for every positive exponent slack. All preprocessing, arithmetic and explicit output costs must fit that proof. A deterministic exact algorithm meeting the time bound is also a positive answer.

A negative answer must rule out all algorithms in the allowed randomized model. Equivalently, for every fixed word constant and program satisfying the termination, feasibility and success requirements, prove that there is some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every size threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid graph encoding with \(N\ge N_0\) and \(\mathbb E[T_A]>C N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The exponent slack may depend on the program. A conditional running-time lower bound must name its unproved assumptions and does not alone establish this unconditional negation.

Algorithms only for bipartite graphs, a near-linear maximal matching, a fixed-accuracy approximation, the optimum size without an output matching, and average performance on random input graphs do not meet the full target. Bounds for pointer machines, parallel rounds, catalytic space or restricted algorithmic techniques must not be substituted for the permitted word-RAM expected time. No additive numerical tolerance applies to either exact optimality or the asymptotic exponent.
cards.why: A major remaining exact graph-optimization problem beyond the almost-linear flow framework. It asks whether odd-cycle and blossom structure impose a real asymptotic cost, even when randomization is allowed.

cards.context:
Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Classical exact algorithms use alternating paths to increase the size of a matching and blossoms to represent the odd-cycle structure of general graphs. Micali and Vazirani's 1980 algorithm has an \(O(m\sqrt n)\) RAM bound on its matching computation, or \(O(n+m\sqrt n)\) when reading all listed isolated vertices is included. Vazirani's later proof distinguishes this from an additional inverse-Ackermann factor in the pointer model. The historical bound is not evidence that such an overhead is necessary for every algorithm.

Bipartite maximum matching reduces to integral unit-capacity maximum flow with \(O(n+m)\) vertices and edges. Chen and coauthors explicitly obtain an almost-linear bipartite matching consequence from their exact flow theorem. Integrality in that setting yields an actual optimum matching. The reduction does not establish the same result on arbitrary undirected graphs, where no bipartition is available and odd-set constraints matter.

A triangle illustrates the integrality issue. Assigning value \(1/2\) to each edge respects a unit bound on the sum incident to every vertex, but has total value \(3/2\), whereas an integral matching has size at most one. For every odd vertex set \(S\), an integral matching contains at most \((|S|-1)/2\) edges entirely inside \(S\). These additional inequalities distinguish the general matching polytope from the simpler bipartite constraints.

Mucha and Sankowski construct maximum matchings by randomized algebraic computation in \(O(n^\omega)\) time for an available matrix-multiplication exponent \(\omega>2\); their Remark 1.1 records an extra logarithmic factor if the exponent is exactly two. Their finite-field arithmetic uses polynomially sized fields. This improves the classical bound on dense graphs, but even a quadratic-in-vertices bound does not approach the explicit input size on sparse graphs.

Duan, Pettie and Su prove a \((1-\delta)\)-approximation for maximum weight matching in \(O(m\delta^{-1}\log\delta^{-1})\) time, so the graph-processing time is linear for fixed \(\delta\). Unit edge weights give the cardinality case, with an additional \(O(n)\) cost for the explicit vertex list. Fixed positive relative error can still allow the loss of many matching edges as \(n\) grows. Making the allowed loss less than one when the optimum is proportional to \(n\) requires inverse-linear accuracy, for which that running-time expression is no longer almost linear.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

A 2011 preprint by Jindal, Kochar and Pal has an abstract claiming \(O(m\log^2 n)\) maximum matching via Glauber dynamics. Its current official arXiv record also contains the authors' correction: the coupling has incorrect marginals, so the mixing-time bound and the main result do not hold. The retained abstract must not be treated as a valid resolution of this target.
